subtopic: DRAFT AGREEMENT FOR UNITED NATIONS RELIEF AND REHABILITATION ADMINISTRATION

speechtext: On the order for motions:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DRAFT AGREEMENT FOR UNITED NATIONS RELIEF AND REHABILITATION ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
On June 11, in reply to an inquiry from the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Graydon), I stated that I hope to be able shortly to lay on the table the draft agreement for the establishment of a United Nations Relief and Rehabilitation Administration. I now table this draft agreement together with an introductory note explaining the status of the proposals. The draft agreement has been framed by the governments of the United States, the United Kingdom, the Soviet Union and China in consultation together. It was presented on June 10 for the consideration of other united nations by the Secretary of State of the United States on behalf of these four powers. It is contemplated that after the other governments have had an opportunity of examining these proposals they will be submitted for discussion and approval to a conference of representatives of the united nations and the nations associated with them in this war. The proposals are now under consideration by the government of Canada and Canada will be glad to send representatives to the projected conference.
The problems of bringing relief and rehabilitation to the war-torn regions of the world as they are liberated from enemy control are so vast as almost to stagger the imagination. Much preparatory work has been done in estimating the requirements in the occupied territories of our European allies and in planning the means for meeting these requirements as far as possible. An inter-allied committee under the chairmanship of Sir Frederick Leith-Ross has been engaged in this task in London for nearly two years. Relief and rehabilitation cover many things in addition to the supply of essential foodstuffs for the restoration and maintenance of health. Clothing and medicines will be urgent needs from the day of liberation. Throughout an essential purpose must be to restore production and commerce in the occupied countries by the provision or repair of means of transport, by the supply of agricultural seeds, machinery and live stock, and by making available essential equipment and raw materials for local industries, es-

Canadian Army-Prize Fighting
pecially those engaged in the manufacture of consumers' goods. Relief in the narrow sense is only the first stage of feeding the hungry, tending the sick, and clothing the needy. Relief merges into rehabilitation- the restoration of the productive capacity of the occupied territories so that they may as soon as possible return to normal economic life.	.
The amounts needed to restore the economies of the occupied countries are very great indeed and the supplies available to the united nations are far from adequate to [DOT] meet all urgent demands. It is, therefore, of the first importance that relief and rehabilitation should be conducted under a carefully planned international scheme, so as to ensure that the best use is made of available supplies and that relief is not denied to those in urgent need because they may lack financial resources or shipping or a stable authority to supervise distribution.
I have already stated that Canada is prepared to play her full part in international relief, and I am sure that this statement is supported in all quarters of this house. Since the draft agreement which I have tabled is tentative and Will be revised in the light of the observations received from many governments, I believe that it is not necessary to discuss its terms at present in any detail. It is a first step in building a united nations organization for this purpose. It would establish at once a council on which all countries participating in the administration would be represented. The council would be supplemented by a central committee, a committee on supplies and regional committees. A director general supported by an international staff would be responsible for executive operation. That is the framework which the agreement would set up. After its establishment, the organs of the united nations relief and rehabilitation administration would work out detailed arrangements within this framework.
For the convenience of hon. members, I suggest that the draft agreement should be printed in Votes and Proceedings of to-day.

subtopic: THIRD ANNIVERSARY OF CALL TO FIGHT-UNION WITH FRENCH ARMIES UNDER GENERAL GIRAUD

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: THIRD ANNIVERSARY OF CALL TO FIGHT-UNION WITH FRENCH ARMIES UNDER GENERAL GIRAUD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 18, 1940 in the darkest hour of this world-wide struggle, a small group of Frenchmen issued a call to their countrymen to continue the fight against the enemy until the hour of final victory. Since that day three years ago the strength and striking power of French
resistance have steadily increased. To-day, the third anniversary of that significant step, would seem to be an appropriate occasion on which to welcome the recent union of the Fighting French Forces of General de Gaulle with the French armies commanded by General Giraud. The formation in North Africa of the French committee of national liberation is a clear indication of the determination of all Frenchmen to work together to bring about the total defeat of the enemy. Though the way will be hard and long we may now look forward, I trust, to the day when France herself will be free and united.

Mr. Speaker, on Friday, June 11, in answer to a question by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon), I stated that I would make inquiries into allegations made by the sports columnist of the Toronto Globe and Mail with reference to arrangements made by the Canadian army respecting Private Johnnie Greco's boxing bouts.
I find that Greco was enlisted on January 13 last and was granted leave without pay from February 5 to February 20 in order to complete a pre-enlistment contract to fight Cleo Shans in New York on February 19. The army had nothing to do with this fight. Following the fight of February 19, Mike Jacobs on behalf of the Twentieth Century Sporting Club of New York asked for a return
Labour Conditions

bout to be held in New York and offered ten per cent of the gross receipts as a gift to military district No. 4 athletic fund. Officers of that district felt that the publicity would be of benefit to the army and Greco was given fourteen days' leave without pay to fight in New York on March 26. The athletic fund of military district No. 4 received $5,000 from the Twentieth Century Sporting Club as its share of the receipts.
As a result of Greco's success in New York it was decided to stage a show in Montreal on May 8. This was completely an army show. All details were handled by officers at military district No. 4 and no civilians were involved. Jacobs had nothing to do with this show except obtaining an opponent for Greco.	He	did	not	share in any of	the
receipts, although indirectly he may have benefited through his connection with Madison Square Gardens by participating in any royalties paid by the American Gillette Razor company for the broadcasting rights.
Greoo received remuneration for the three fights.	For	his	fight	in Montreal he	got
$2,328, out of which he would have to pay his trainer, also training and incidental expenses. Military district No. 4 athletic fund got $1,586, clear of all expenses, out of the Montreal fight.
Officers in military district No. 4 felt that the Canadian army was receiving favourable publicity by Greco's fights. Consequently when the Twentieth Century Sporting Club offered	him	an	opportunity to fight	BobMontgomery	in	New	York the offer	was
accepted, subject to the exigencies of the service and to permission being given by National Defence headquarters for Greco to go to New York to fight. Permission was refused, so that the fight will not take place.

tylr. QUELCH: Could the minister give the committee any information regarding the grasshopper situation in western Canada? We are informed that there is likely to be a serious infestation in various parts of the west.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) :
speechtext: It is not expected that the situation will be at all serious this year. As hon. members from the west are aware, it is not usual for us to have very bad infestations under conditions such as we had last year, or following last year's conditions.
I understand from a recent crop report that certain parts of eastern Alberta are very dry.
Of course, in any limited localities where there are difficulties they will be taken care of, as usual, by arrangements between this department and the departments in Alberta.

Are there any new developments in this department? It has done a great deal of good work in connection with the potato industry in New Brunswick. Has the minister anything to report in that connection? I understand that the late director, Doctor Gibson, has been retired on superannuation and that a successor has been appointed.
So far as Doctor Gibson is concerned, Doctor L. S. McLaine is taking his place.

Yes, I understand that. What I want to know is whether the minister has anything to report in the way of progress made last year. In my view this is an important service. Has he anything interesting to tell the country?

There is nothing at present which would warrant a special statement with regard to this particular section. The

Supply-Agriculture
usual work, of course, is going on, and a little later in the season, because of some investigations which are now being held, a statement will be made.

Has the minister had any report on an infestation which is affecting the elm trees in my city? Does the department take cognizance of that sort of thing-tent caterpillars and the like- and what help do they lend to treatment?
The laboratory which deals with that matter is located in Fredericton.
Yes.
And of course they examine into all difficulties which arise in connection with trees or forests in general and make reports on them, and efforts are made to combat such difficulties as exist.

Can the minister give us any information as to what progress has been made towards coping with the infestation of the hardwood trees in eastern Canada, and also the sawfly infestation in our eastern forests? A great deal of damage has been done to the hardwood growths; hundreds of thousands of dollars have been lost, I am afraid, by reason of these infestations. The department was taking steps to combat both. Has the minister anything to report?

I suppose it is the bronze birch borer which is referred to. My understanding is that there has not been discovered any means of combating the attacks that are made by the borer on hardwood trees, but that the department assists in salvaging the wood which is affected as a result of the operations of this insect.

Is the department continuing investigations of ways and means of combating it? What progress if any has been made beyond the mere negative which the minister has indicated? This is very important; the infestation is the source of great loss, as I tried to emphasize a moment ago. Has the same situation been met in the United States; what, if anything, has been done down there; and are we utilizing all available sources of information from the continent if there are any such now? Germany used to be very much alive to this sort of thing, but I suppose that source of information is now dried up. No progress has been made; in effect that is what the minister tells us?
That is quite right.
I am sorry to hear it.
The work has been going on continuously, but we have not yet discovered any means of successfully combating the borer.

What
about the sawfly? Some years ago a parasite was imported. Has that experiment been successful; that is, in connection with the spruce?

Yes, Mr. Chairman. The method of fighting that particular insect has been described to the house, I think, each session since I have been down here, and probably for some time before that. The scourge has spread over a very considerable part of the area, particularly in the eastern part of Canada, and we have been breeding parasites and distributing them. I understand that some 800 millions have been distributed, and the insect seems to be under control. The scourge is gradually being reduced in different parts.
That is to say, the infestation is not spreading?
No, it is not spreading; it is being reduced rather than increasing.

This year, throughout
Canada, and particularly in the west, the people responded to the idea of victory gardens, but I understand there has been quite an infestation of the cutworm. I had a letter yesterday from a correspondent who said that this year he put in about another acre of garden to produce vegetables, because of the appeal which was made to do something in that line, but practically the whole thing has been destroyed. He wound up his letter with the words, "No more victory garden for me." Will the minister state what information he has with respect to the cutworm, what damage it has done, and what steps are being taken to deal with it?
The cutworm, of course, is always present, particularly in western Canada, whether they are victory gardens or whether they are not. Cutworms do not pay much attention to that.
They do not make any discrimination.

No; and at times they become so plentiful that they destroy the crops as well as the gardens. I am not aware that there is any serious infestation this year in connection with crops, but I have no doubt that considerable destruction has taken place, as usual, in gardens. The only thing I can say with regard to dealing with them is that in the experience of the past there has been a
Supply-Agriculture

fly which has usually followed the cutworm and which acts in somewhat the same way as any parasite acts upon any of these different pests that we have. The fly darts around and lays an egg in the cutworm which results .n the cutworm itself being consumed. That goes on continuously; it is a peculiarity with insect life. I do not know what can be done about the cutworm in gardens, unless one goes out in the garden and sees to it that they are destroyed with poison or otherwise.

I understand that some damage has been caused by the mountain pine bark beetle. Does that come under the supervision of the Department of Agriculture, and if so, how many men are engaged in combating this pest? What success are they having?

The work is directed by the entomological branch, as is all work done in connection with insects and grubs. The men are provided for that particular task in that area by the mines and resources department, and it becomes a matter of forestry. I am not sure about the number of men employed in the work, but the work is being carried on.

Has the minister any
information as to the importance of the work and what the consequence is likely to be if this pest is not controlled?

If the insect is not controlled it will do a great deal of damage, more particularly to the scenic aspects of that particular area. Much of the pine is jackpine and is not as valuable commercially as some other varieties of pine, but the damaging of any timber anywhere must be controlled if at all possible. I understand that this particular parasite is under control and is not doing as much damage as it would otherwise.

I wish to call the attention of the Minister of Agriculture to an advertisement appearing in a recent issue of the Herald of Hanna, Alberta, under the heading "Sylvatic Plague." A map is shown of the area affected, north, east and south, and for further information readers are directed to write either to the department of health or to the department cf entomology. In my opinion this is more a matter for the entomological branch than for [DOT] the department of health. I quote the advertisement :
Warning
All persons residing, or entering within, the areas shown on the accompanying map are hereby informed:
1.	That gophers, and gopher-fleas, infected with sylvatic plague are present in these areas.
2.	That sylvatic plague is a very serious human disease.

3.	That it is possible for man to contact sylvatic plague by handling infected animals or through the bite of an infected flea.
4.	That vaccination against sylvatic plague is not feasible at present.
5.	That the only method of control of sylvatic plague in nature is by the control of the gophers.
6.	That control of gophers requires a systematic gopher poisoning campaign on each farmstead.
7.	That it is imperative that all residents within the infected areas take the following steps to protect their health and welfare.
(a)	Do not handle living or dead gophers. Gophers found dead should be buried.
(b)	A well-organized "gopher control" campaign using a recognized gopher poison should be carried out on each farmstead. Particular attention should be paid to effective poisoning on the land surrounding the buildings.
This disease is going to spread unless effective action is taken to control it. As a matter of fact it has already spread, and the areas affected are in townships from 24 to 30 miles apart. The farmers in these areas are too sparsely settled to carry out an effective poisoning campaign, and if we are to depend upon them to kill the gophers these animals will not be destroyed. I suggest that the army could very well be utilized for this purpose. In the district south of Hanna in the Tilley area a great deal of work is being carried on experimentally with gas, and I should imagine that gas would be the best means that could be used for destroying gophers in an area of that size, which is 66 square miles. These fleas can 'be carried by stock or by human beings. Evidence of this may be found in the fact that men carrying on investigational work travel in a car equipped with a bath and as soon as they have finished their field work they take a bath. But invariably they find a number of fleas on their clothes, and these fleas can give the plague. If the fleas are carried out of the area on live stock the disease may spread to other parts of Canada. I suggest that we should do everything in our power to destroy this menace while it is still confined to a limited area. Would it not be possible for the federal government to cooperate with the province in a systematic campaign for the purpose of destroying the gophers? I repeat, if you depend on the farmers to destroy the animals they will not be destroyed and the plague will gradually spread over various parts of the west.

The work that is being done in this direction is being carried on in the health department and not under this department. I am not sure what the arrangements are between the health authorities in the province and the administration here, but work has been going on for two years constantly.

Supply-Agriculture
They have the assistance of our entomologists but the work is really paid for and directed by the Department of Health. I think it would be more helpful to the hon. member if he would discuss it when the estimates of the Minister of Health are before the committee.

But the department of health would have to depend on the Department of Agriculture for the campaign to destroy the gophers. It is hardly within the purview of the department of health to poison gophers.

The men out there from the department of health are making a study of the disease itself, the means by which it spreads, and methods whereby it can be avoided. The information thus obtained will be reported to those persons who will use it for the purpose of destroying as far as possible the gophers and the fleas.

I understand that so far the work done is merely investigational. They have not themselves carried out any work for the destruction of the gophers. They have recommended that the farmers should destroy them but no action has been taken to institute a campaign for the wholesale destruction of these animals. The farmers are not doing it, because in many areas they are operating several thousands of acres and one farmer could not possibly poison such a vast area.

Investigational work will be carried on by the health department, but the work necessary to combat the disease would, I should think, be carried out by the provincial authorities rather than by the federal department either of agriculture or of health. Matters having to do with health are largely under the administration of the province, and that is true of the destruction of gophers. It is not under my administration but under .provincial administration; I am quite sure, however, that the authorities in Alberta are alive to the situation and will deal with it, as it is their duty to do. However, if representations are made here and any assistance can be given by any of our people it will always be given.

May I ask the minister t;o give some description, not in detail, of the work which this plant protection branch of science service actually accomplishes? I believe we had an item before us on a previous
occasion, but I am not sure that we have ever had a detailed description of the work for which this vote actually provides.

When we were in
committee a week ago, discussing item 3, the minister said he would table the report of the advisory committee on agricultural services. He said there was a report, and that before going into committee again it would be tabled.
The only thing available is the minutes of the meetings of the advisory committee. However, I shall make a further check.

Item agreed to.
Experimental farms service.
12. Experimental farms administration, $59,480.

Speaking in the house last March I said that when the agricultural estimates were under consideration I intended to move an amendment asking for the allocation of S500.000 to be appropriated by the dominion government for agricultural research in Canada. Looking over the estimates I see no point at which within the rules I could move an amendment of the kind. Perhaps my purpose will' be better served if, instead of endeavouring to -move an amendment, I initiate a discussion on the subject.

The ihon. member is
not surrendering his position?

No, not a bit;
if the leader of the opposition can show me where my amendment can be properly moved, I shall move it,

That is your job, not
mine.

As I said in
March, in Canada we have not gone very far in the matter of agricultural research. Our experimental farms and our departments of agriculture across the country have done much excellent work in connection with production services, the dissemination of information on cultural methods, the health of animals, the oreeding of animals, plant breeding and many other subjects of great interest to agriculturists in Canada. But as yet we have not done any real work in respect of at least two phases which require careful study. One has to do with agricultural research in order further to develop ways and means of distributing foodstuffs throughout the world, and the other has to do with finding ways and means of using agricultural products and byproducts in industry.

In the United States during the past few years four great agricultural research laboratories have been set up. We would do well to follow the United States in that particular. I hold in my hand an article which deals with the different agricultural research laboratories in the United States. It points out that a northern laboratory was established at Peoria, Illinois, a southern at New Orleans, an eastern at Wyndmoor, near Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, and a western in southern California, near San Francisco. The article states:
When congress provided for the establishment of these laboratories it made clear the type of research it had in mind, and stated it in the act as follows:
"The Secretary of Agriculture is hereby authorized and directed to establish, equip and maintain four regional research laboratories, one in each major farm producing area, and, at such laboratories, to conduct researches into and to develop new scientific, chemical and technical uses, and new and extended markets and outlets for farm commodities and products and byproducts thereof. Such research and development shall be devoted primarily to those farm commodities in which there are regular or seasonal surpluses, and their products and by-products.
We would do well to follow the example of the United States in this -regard. There are four sections in Canada which should have the services of laboratories. The maritime provinces would compose one section, the central provinces of Ontario and Quebec a second, the three prairie provinces a third, and British Columbia a fourth. In all these areas different types of agriculture are carried on, and there is great scope in all four for work to be done in agricultural research.
First, in regard to foods, we should be able through research to find out and to set up grades and standards which have for their basis complete information from analyses as to the food value of products, their chemical constituents and vitamin values, as -well as their nutritional content. Through research we can also find new methods of transportation, cold storage and the handling of farm products for export; the handling of fresh foods, storage conditions, distribution methods and packaging; quick freezing and dehydration methods and the preserving of foods both commercially and for domestic use.
In these different laboratories I suggest that in the maritime provinces, for instance, research work could be done in connection with fruits, potatoes, legumes, grasses, marsh grasses, plastics and substitutes for building materials. In that laboratory a great deal of very necessary information could be gained by studying fish, fish products, fish oils, sea foods and by-products thereof. In Ontario and

Supply-Agriculture
Quebec work could be done on tobacco, corn, animal fats and oils, skins., hides and tanning, vegetable products, fruits, soybeans, fibre flax, milkweed, milk products, beans and peas. In the western provinces the work might include corn, wheat, coarse grains, oil seeds, a fermentation pilot plant for the purpose of discovering uses of derivatives from different grains, chemical uses of starch, the development of butylene glycol, sugars, glucose and the industrial uses of starch, alcohols and organic acids.
Does that list cover alfalfa?

Not in the
west; that comes under legumes and grasses in the maritimes.
Of course you have alfalfa in Saskatchewan.
Yes, but we grow it for seed more than anything else, while in eastern Canada it is grown more for feed or for sale.
What about bees in the west? The problem is different there than in the east, I believe.

I believe these
different laboratories should cooperate with each other, so that the work being done in one would be made known to the others. I am simply laying out certain things that I think might be dealt with in the different laboratories throughout Canada. In British Columbia they might study apples, all types of fruits both small and large, vegetables, milk and milk products, grasses and legumes, seeds, seed crops and the residue from seed crops which are grown in British Columbia; drug plants, which are starting to be grown there; poultry products and by-products and again fish and sea food by-products. The industrial uses of all these by-products in the various parts of Canada could be worked out in the different laboratories.
I do not intend to detain the committee or the minister longer in regard to this matter. I think we are long past the time in this country, with agriculture such an important industry, when we should have expended large sums of money for the purposes I have mentioned. The amount I asked, $500,000, is a very small amount for this purpose; it is only a start. I intimated also that I thought the different provinces of Canada should help by putting up smaller amounts, and also that industry in Canada should be willing to help by giving perhaps a couple of hundred thousand dollars a year to this work, because
they too would benefit greatly by the things which might be found out during the course of the work carried on in these laboratories.
I bring up this matter under the Department of Agriculture, knowing that for years we have had a research bureau here in Ottawa, which has done excellent work. Unfortunately for the agriculturist in Canada, however-and this is my opinion-with the laboratory located here in the centre of the industrial area of Canada, quite properly the men in charge have endeavoured to work out the problems that have been placed upon their desks day by day. Therefore to a large extent the problems of industry have been worked out while the problems of the agriculturist have not been properly placed before the bureau here in Ottawa. I think therefore the only way to have this work carried on is to have a separate branch altogether, with money voted for it separately, in order that agriculture might set up its own research bureaus and carry on its own research work. No doubt certain men who are to-day connected with the national research bureau would be taken into these new bureaus, and they would be very good men because already they have done valuable work for agriculture in Canada. We have never had a set-up under which a sufficient number of scientists could be brought together in a laboratory in Canada to work on agricultural products, knowing that from one year to the next they could carry on and the money would be provided.
Is there any comprehensive work of this kind being carried on in any of the provinces now, to my hon. friend's knowledge?
No great amount, though some work is being done in connection with the research bureau by various agricultural colleges and universities throughout the country.
I had in mind soil testing, for instance.

Yes, that is done in different provinces, but I am endeavouring to visualize the large programme that is very necessary to this country, and I think my hon. friend agrees that we should start now. Only to-day the Prime Minister made a statement in regard1 to food after the war. We are not going far enough in endeavouring to find out the things we should find out right now in order that when this war is over we may be able to produce, dehydrate and transport the foods it will be necessary to send to hungry people in other parts
S upply-A griculture

of the world. These are all things that can be worked out in laboratories of the type I have mentioned.
Would it be my hon. friend's idea that this scheme should be coordinated with the facilities that exist at the present time in the various provinces?

Absolutely; I
think we should cooperate with anyone in order to get everything possible done. I am sure any laboratories set up by the Department of Agriculture would be only too glad to cooperate with any scientific men throughout the dominion, whether employed by industry or by the provinces.

As I understand the
hon. member's plan, it would have to be a dominion-provincial scheme.

It would have to be started by somebody, and I believe this is the place to start it. In conclusion I want to say that I hope other hon. members, who I know are as much interested as I am in this thing, will stand up in their places this afternoon so that we may have a [DOT] real expression of opinion on this question. The government will then realize that something of this kind should be done in Canada at the present time.

I may have something further to say at a later stage in this discussion. Those of us who come from rural areas are naturally interested in any scheme to improve the position of the farmer. The hon. member referred to this matter earlier in the session, and again on March 17. At that time we were encouraged to think that he was going to make a determined drive upon the government. He took a vigorous stand and said, as reported on page 1330 of Hansard:
When we reach the agricultural estimates it is my intention to move an amendment which I hope the government will see fit to accept.
I am sorry to have seen the member adopt a, compromising attitude this afternoon. When he retreated from the strong position which he took on March 17-perhaps it was because it was March 17 that he took that position -I would have preferred that he did so because under the rules of the house a private member is not permitted to move an amendment which will increase the estimates. However, evidently that is not his idea, because he has just taken the position that he will do what he has done so many times-make a recommendation to the government.
I should have liked the hon. member to give us further particulars of his plan, to which no doubt he has given considerable

study. Over the years there has been a gradual development in agriculture along the lines of technical research, and farming to-day is a vastly different thing from what it was yesterday. The agricultural industry, however, is a long way behind many other industries in connection with the return obtained for the labour and management and capital invested. These are matters which can be dealt wdth at a more appropriate time. Farmers and farm labour have seen fit to trek to other lines of endeavour where there are more appropriate returns. Having that thought definitely in mind, the question of a greater production from the same amount of labour becomes a matter of considerable importance.
The question raised by the hon. member with respect to scientific experiments and varied uses of farm products is an important one, but how best we can accomplish it is something which will have to receive considerable study. We must get the best out of any plan that is proposed. Many hon. members who are farmers no doubt will be able to express themselves better than I and from a greater experience, but I think they will agree that in many instances the farmer who has made the most money or has achieved the greatest material success has been the man who has engaged in some specialized type of farming which perhaps has not been subject to the same competition as other lines. This has been demonstrated to me by several farmers whom I know well, many old neighbours of ours on the farm. Keeping that definitely in mind, it seems to me that there is a place for the scheme the hon. member proposed.
I am not finding fault with the minister or with his splendid department, but the fact is that agricultural research is a long way behind. More consideration will have to be given, perhaps under the leadership of the dominion government, to scientific farm research. When the hon. member was speaking I threw in one or two interjections with regard to the position of the existing facilities in the various provinces which have been attempting on a smaller scale to deal wdth the problems mentioned by the hon. member. In carrying out a scheme such as is envisaged by the hon. member I think it is essential that the department of the government more particularly involved should confer with the provinces in order that there may be proper coordination and cooperation.
Agriculture has been behind other industries in scientific and laboratory experiments. There is a good reason for this. In many instances industry has been in position to

Supply-Agriculture
spend considerable sums of private money upon scientific research for the development of the particular industry. But in the past, and at pres'ent, our farmers have not been and are not in that position. Most farmers have a difficult enough time now to get along, to pay their debts, to educate their children, to carry on their normal pursuits of life without having anything extra left over to undertake any experimentation or laboratory work. I think all of us can recall instances where particular industries have made considerable progress along scientific lines, but unfortunately agriculture has not had the same opportunities.
If I understood correctly the theme of the hon. member's address this afternoon it is that we should provide for agriculture the same opportunities that are given to industry in order to bring about greater returns. At the proper time the minister and his assistants will be able to give us the necessary technical information. Everything possible should be done to help the farmer along these lines and to at least put him in a position nearer to that of industry. I know of no reason why the farmers of this country should not enjoy the same advantages and opportunities as other industries. On these general lines I am strongly in favour of the suggestion which has been made by the hon. member for Moose Jaw. I think my views are stronger, if possible, than his on this subject, and I was sorry that he started off with such high power only to land up in low gear, as he did this afternoon.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson) is going to place our joint view before the house in order to shorten the discussion. I shall content myself by saying that we strongly support the request that has been made by the member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross) that a special appropriation be made for conducting this important experimental work. He has quoted from United States records showing to some extent what has been done in that country, but to save time he quoted, I think, only in part. We know the tremendous amount of work that can be done along this line, and we are glad to support in every respect the request he made this afternoon.

Mr. Chairman, I think the member for Moose Jaw has placed the house and the country in his debt by opening up this important subject. I recall that during the early thirties, when wheat was selling at the lowest price in history, the federal government of the day, assisted by the Saskatchewan government, spent large sums of money to bring people from the drought area to the
north country to produce more wheat. If half a million dollars had been spent at that time in trying to devise new uses for agricultural products something much more useful would have been accomplished, because many people who were established on farms in the west during the thirties have left the farms and the investment made has been a complete loss in many cases to the federal and provincial authorities.
Members of the committee who would like to have up-to-date information on this interesting subject of chemurgy I feel sure could obtain it from the Saskatchewan Industrial Development board, which issues publications from time to time. I hold in my hand one of their circulations which contains a report of an address given by Thomas B. Hill, Secretary of the Department of Conservation and Development, Olympia, Washington. For the benefit of those who are not familiar with this interesting subject, he explains at the outset what chemurgy is all about. He says:
Farm chemurgy is chemistry at work on farm products. Heretofore there has been something very scientific about the word to the lay public, and the average person has been inclined to shy away from it. But chemurgy is neither too scientific, nor is there anything mysterious about it. As a matter of fact it is thoroughly practical, and the public in becoming familiar with it is finding out that it means the utilization in industry of surplus and waste crops, and the development of specialty crops.
He goes on to tell of the place of the soybean in our modem economy, and says:
Less than ten years ago practically no soybeans were being produced in this country. So rapidly was it developed as an industrial raw material, that in 1941, 5,855,000 acres were devoted to the crops, with a production of over 100,000,000 bushels. So great had become the demand for soybean products that for 1942 the farmers of the United States were urged to plant 9,000,000 acres to the crop. Here we have nine million acres of farm land devoted to a crop that was unknown ten years ago. The crushing of the beans to obtain the oil and meal, and the manufacturing of the various by-products, constitute a large industrial operation.
I know that a good deal of experimental work has been done in Canada, but what has been accomplished in the United States shows how important it is to spend a considerable sum of money on experimental work.
Here is another interesting fact given in Mr. Hill's address:
Comparatively few people know that a fur made from casein, a milk product, is being used in place of rabbit fur in the manufacture of men's felt hats. The extent to which it has thus been used in the last two or three years is astounding. There has been a shortage of rabbit fur, which comes largely from England, Scotland, New Zealand and Australia, because of the war. It is estimated that 50,000,000 felt
Supply-Agriculture

hats were made from casein in 1941. Now that a shortage in milk is developing, chemurgy no doubt will produce some other product to take the place of rabbit and casein fur.
I also have here the publication "So That Man May Prosper", from which the hon. member for North Battleford quoted extensively the other night when speaking of synthetic rubber. I shall not take time to make any comment on the reply which the Minister of Munitions and Supply made to the statements in this publication, but I would draw attention to three or four developments dealt with by the author, Mr. Dyson Carter, in this publication. He of course spends a good deal of time in discussing industrial alcohol and I feel sure that the future will demonstrate that wheat and other agricultural products can be used successfully in the manufacture of synthetic rubber.
Mr. Dyson Carter also has an interesting article on plastics. He says:
Hundreds of thousands of tons of straw and similar material goes to waste on our farms every year-the largest garbage pile in the country. Several processes have been developed to make plastics from straw. Iowa State College scientists have perfected such a plastic m several forms, with the cost as low as 44 cents a pound. This is about half the price of the cheapest plastic now on the market. The Iowa material can be made into practically any shape or size of product. In large slabs it can compete with the better grades of lumber for construction purposes.
There is also a section on cloth, from which I quote:
In one process developed by the Ford Motor Company scientists, soybean meal (after the oil has been extracted) is chemically treated so that it becomes liquid. This liquid is handled just as liquid rayon-it is sprayed into a chemical bath, in which the fine jets of liquid instantly turn into firm threads. These threads can be made to resemble either silk or wool. The "soy threads" are at present being woven and knitted, and the cloth is being marketed in the United States for hat felts, suitings, upholstery fabrics, etc.
He tells of several other developments in connection with soybean industries and of new uses for flax and deals with dandelion rubber. Of the latter he says:
For twenty years Russian scientists and practical farmers have studied the problem of growing natural rubber in cold climates. The tropical rubber tree will not survive. But there are other plants that produce rubber. Among these are Guayule and Kok-Sagyz.
I understand that the minister intends to make a statement on the problem of growing rubber, to which Mr. Dyson Carter devotes half a page in this publication.
Furfural is also discussed, and several miscellaneous projects, such as the wallboard industry, the manufacture of new types of

cements, fuel for heating rural homes. The subjects which are discussed by Mr. Dyson Carter in this publication suggest a wide field for study if an appropriation were made such as the hon. member for Moose Jaw suggests. I think he is very modest in asking for only half a million dollars. That does not seem to go very far in these days. When one thinks of the future of western Canada and the importance of finding new uses for agricultural products grown on those plains, the Minister of Agriculture would be wise, I think, to bring in an estimate next year, or as the hon. member for Vancouver East suggests, a supplementary estimate this year, appropriating at least half a million dollars for the purpose of carrying on this experimental work. I am sure that an appropriation such as the hon. member for Moose Jaw proposed would meet with the support of members on this side and of members on the government benches.

I wish to support the suggestion which the hon. member for Moose Jaw has made to the minister. The speech which the hon. member for Moose Jaw made earlier in the session aroused a great deal of interest in my community. I had many comments upon it, all to the effect that for a downright, honest, practical suggestion that actually would bring results to the farmer, the suggestion made by the hon. member for Moose Jaw took the cake. I am passing this compliment on to him because I know that the people of Brant were much interested in the contribution he made in this speech. It revived their belief that those who are championing the cause of agriculture include at least one man who has touched upon something which gives ground for hope in the future. Since the hon. member made that speech I have discussed the problem with many persons who are interested in the subject. In my opinion there is a great opportunity for those who are prepared to interest themselves in finding new outlets for the products of the farm. I know of no better way of encouraging agriculture.
May I say that I am not sure I agree with the leader of the opposition in his remark that the only prosperous farmer is the farmer who specializes.
No, Mr. Chairman, that is not what I said.
I understood the hon. gentleman to say that in the great majority of cases the prosperity of our rural people depends upon specialist farming.

No; I said that those who interest themselves in special lines of farming

Supply

Agriculture
find themselves in perhaps a little better position to be assured of better returns than those who do not.

Well, I think the hon. member and I are very much on common ground. It is true that some specialty farmers have made an unqualified success, but it will be found, I believe, that there have been more financial disasters among those who, in pursuing some special line, put all their eggs in one basket. From experience in my own community I would rather say that the average well-to-do farmer is the man engaged in mixed farming, because if one line fails him he has some other to fall back on. No doubt there are exceptions to all rules; I do not know that either my own viewpoint or that of the leader of the opposition proves invariably correct. There are specialists who have made successes as well as those who have made failures; probably the same applies in the case of mixed farming.
The hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson) spoke of the value of straw, and suggested that it was one of the articles which in this country is most often wasted. So far as Ontario is concerned, my view is that it is a mistake to let straw leave the farm. I do not believe you can get any return from straw which you dispose of that will compensate for its value when applied to the soil.

I believe everyone in
eastern Canada will agree with what the hon. member says on that particular point. Actually most of the farm leases contain a clause that straw must not leave the farm. As my hon. friend knows, there is very good reason for that provision.

I appreciate the reference of the leader of the opposition to the legal aspect of this matter. There is no doubt that the purpose of inserting that clause in the contract is to protect the fertility of the farm.
Attention was called in the agriculture committee this morning to what has been achieved by disposing of a by-product of the flax mills to the pulp mills, thereby converting 500 carloads this year into various grades of paper. There is one case where research has made use of something which would otherwise have gone to waste. It leads me to recommend to the minister that, in case a research bureau is decided upon, it should cooperate with industry, which already has many research laboratories of its own. A young chemical engineer in one of the food companies whose parent company is in the United States drew my attention to the great possibilities which exist in
cooperation with industry, and I believe that industry would welcome the opportunity to cooperate with the government. If we can set them a specific job to do, as they have the necessary equipment and very considerable experience, we may possibly obtain results which will benefit not only the farmer and the industrialist but the nation at large. That is a field wherein we can start something immediately, without incurring any great additional cost, by simply utilizing facilities which are already available.
There are other directions in which such a bureau could enlarge its efforts. I have often wondered why farmers, while so anxious to purchase labour-saving machinery for the production of field crops, completely neglect opportunities of labour saving arrangements in so designing their buildings as to facilitate the doing of work which has to be done every morning, noon and night in the care and feeding of live stock. It seems to me that we have a great field there for planned agricultural architecture. Some people may be inclined to say, let the farmer erect his buildings any way he wants them; it is he who has to do the chores. But in my experience most farmers are only too glad to receive suggestions from those who can assist them, and I believe they would welcome architectural designs for application to farm buildings which would assist them in feeding their stock with less labour and take some of the drudgery out of their lives. In that way, this particular bureau might make an important contribution to the happiness of life on the farm.
I wish now only to emphasize my appreciation, and that of many others with whom I have spoken, of the contribution which the hon. member for Moose Jaw has made to this subject. We hope it will bear fruit.

At the risk of appearing
somewhat old fashioned, or even reactionary, I should like to express myself on the subject which is under discussion. I believe I have some qualifications, because before beginning to farm in Canada now some forty years ago, I happen to have studied analytical chemistry in England. If I have not the respect for science that some members seem to have, as a solution for our troubles, it may be the result of my long experience. I remember a few years ago wandering through our experimental farm here in Ottawa and coming on some men in a laboratory. I asked them what they were doing, and they told me they were experimenting with cider. They were trying to make a really good cider with Canadian apples. I asked them if there was
Supply-Agriculture

any difficulty about that. They said, "We have tried apples from different parts of the country, from Prince Edward Island to Vancouver island, but so far we have not been able to find an apple which when fermented will retain the flavour of the apple." They had a number of samples of cider and they kindly gave me a glass. They asked me my opinion of it, and I said, "Well, it is a long time since I left home, but as far as I can remember that seems to me pretty fair cider." One man said to me, "Yes, that is all right; but one-third of the apples came from England." I said to him, "I know something of analytical chemistry and I don't think you will find a solution to that problem in any test-tube." He admitted that he did not think they would. I said, "I will give you another instance. You cannot make Devonshire cream outside Devonshire." Probably my hon. friend will bear me out in this. This scientist on the experimental farm said, "Yes; that is true, I know it, because I lived in Somerset before coming to Canada and we used to make Devonshire cream and sell it. You can make it in the west of England but nowhere else. I thought I would make it when I got to Canada and that I might do very well out of it. I tried it in Nova Scotia. They can make Devonshire cream, yes, but it has no flavour." The same in British Columbia. Friends of mine are Devonshire people and they make Devonshire cream. It looks the same, but there is no flavour. That is the fault of it.
I mention these things just to show that science is not the entire answer to these problems. Agriculture is more than a science; it is an art. People seem to think that we know more about farming through science than our forefathers did a hundred years ago, but in my humble opinion we have forgotten a great deal that they knew then and I think we have to go back and rediscover a lot of the knowledge they had.
I understand that in England it has been rediscovered that by and large, generally speaking, the health of human beings depends more than anything else on the food they eat, the quality of the food; and that again depends on the health of the soil in which that food is grown. You cannot maintain the 'proper health of the soil through chemical manure. I understand they tried increasing the yield of tobacco in Cuba-of course that is not food-by means of chemical manures, and immediately the quality of the tobacco was found to be very much lower. They are coming to the conclusion in England and elsewhere I suppose, that we shall have to go back to the immemorial customs of China

and India, where the soil has been farmed not for half a century but for a thousand years. It is done by the age-old method of returning to the soil what is taken out of it. But that by the way.
I do not wish to throw cold water on the idea, and I think there is room for a scheme of the kind which the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross) has put before the house. But I am wondering whether the main idea behind it is not really economic rather than chemical. Is it not the idea that by turning food or the edible products of the soil into inedible products such as rubber-which I think is pretty hard chewing-it will be possible to raise prices through overcoming the so-called abundance of agricultural products? To me, if this research station is established it would seem desirable that at the same time and perhaps in the same building there be included some really new economists, not the orthodox or even eminent economists, but some really scientific economists who will see what faults there are in the present economic system whereby, though there is a so-called overproduction of food, millions of people in the world are at the same time underfed and undernourished.
The main problem is economic rather than chemical. What we have to do is to increase the purchasing power of the people so that at least they can consume food to the limits of their desires or of our powers to produce. I do not altogether feel comfortable about the idea of turning edible products into chemical substances. I realize of course that in war time, when there is an emergency, everything must give way to the demands of war. You may say that a few million bushels of wheat would provide us with a certain quantity of rubber, but that would be only the beginning. I wonder what the development would be in a hundred years time if we pursued these lines, where the soil is put to the use of producing and supplying industry rather than human stomachs.
I am not comfortable about that and I rose simply to make these observations to the committee. I want to emphasize my belief that the main problem before agriculture, although I do not know that the minister will agree with me, is economic rather than scientific. If the farmer is provided with a really good market and satisfactory prices he can be left to find his own solution for the raising of the best food in the best possible way.

It was not my intention to say anything on this very important subject. What I have to say could have been said on another item. But what the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross) has brought before

Supply-Agriculture
the committee, namely, the subject of agricultural research in all its phases, is of very considerable importance, and perhaps I would do well to say a few words. I had intended to say something respecting the improvement of the health and state of our pure-bred cattle in general. Possibly that is a subject which might well be discussed now.
I listened to the hon. member for Wetaski-win (Mr. Jaques) when he spoke about Devonshire cream. That is something I had never heard of until about a month ago. However I had some of this product known as Devonshire cream at the house of an Englishman who lives just north of Winnipeg. It was made from the milk of Aberdeen Angus cows I had sold him just a few years earlier.
We have in Hull an institution known as the animal diseases research institute. Undoubtedly this branch has done some good work, but in my opinion it has not advanced as rapidly as it .should have, nor has it dealt as extensively as it should have with conditions pertaining to live stock. My concern to-day is with a disease known as Bang's disease, or contagious abortion in cattle. I have had many years' experience in the cattle business, and particularly in the pure-bred branch of the business. Every breeder knows that sometimes he will run up against this menace. Not only is it a menace to cattle but it is also a menace to the health of one's own family and to people in general. It is, therefore, of the utmost importance that something be done to find a real, practical and efficient method of ascertaining the cause and finding some remedy for its eradication.
For -the information of hon. members I should like to record an experience I had. Some years ago I sold a consignment of cattle, subject to test for Bang's disease. Some of those cattle reacted. Of course hon. members will understand that those cattle were not taken; they remained in my herd. I was not very much concerned about that, because they had been one hundred per cent producers each year. Some of them were nine years old and had produced as many as seven calves. The fact that the sale was cut, however, did cause me some concern, and is the concern of producers who are breeding cattle to-day. Because unless one has a certified Bang's-disease-free herd, or the herd passes the test for Bang's disease, he cannot do much business. One cannot do business either on the other side of the boundary line, or in some of the provinces in Canada. There are breeders throughout Canada who will not buy cattle unless they have passed successfully the Bang's disease test.
I wanted to do a little experimenting. For years I had been reading about the ravages of Bang's disease, and the attempts of different breeders and different governments to try to control them. I had read that in the experiment being made, blood samples had been taken from cattle, that the identical samples had been sent to several laboratories, and that the results of tests had been different in each case. I wondered just what confidence breeders could have in a test of that kind. In carrying out my experiment I asked my son, when in one year he was having our cattle tested for tuberculosis, to have a sample of blood taken from two cows which had reacted two years earlier. I took those two samples, sending one to Doctor Savage, our own animal pathologist in Winnipeg, and another to the laboratory in Hull. My purpose was to have a check, to ascertain whether the two laboratories would show the same results on the test. In regard to the test taken in Winnipeg-and it will be remembered that a test had been taken two or three years earlier- the positive finding was confirmed. The same day I sent exactly the same blood to the pathologist in Hull, Doctor E. A. Watson, and this was the reply I received:
Messrs. Harry Leader & Son,
Portage la Prairie,
Manitoba.
Dear sir,
I am in receipt of two blood samples submitted by you and wish to advise you that blood tests, for the diagnosis of Bang's disease, are conducted at this institute under the following circumstances only:
A.	Cattle in herds accepted by the health of animals division, production services, as under their supervision for the control and eradication of Bang's disease; and cattle as replacements or additions to such herds.
B.	Cattle selected for export from the Dominion of Canada.
C.	Cattle selected for shows and exhibitions at which a blood test is a necessary requirement for their admittance.
Yours truly,
E. A. Watson,
Dominion Animal Pathologist.
I can see no reason why they could not have tested the samples in Hull. I went to a lot of trouble to send -those samples by special mail delivery, so that they would reach Hull in plenty of time. However, the reply I received was that they did not have authority to test the samples. I believed they did. If the laboratory at Hull had confirmed the test in Winnipeg my confidence would have -been revived. If the tests had been different, as is indicated in what I have read, then I would
Supply-Agriculture

have been just as anxious as I am to-day to see that we get something which would be more workable.
Breeders are becoming more and more concerned about Bang's disease. They are willing to cooperate with this or any other government in any workable plan for the protection of cattle. I- do not know what the annual loss is in Canada, but it has been estimated that the annual loss in the United States from the ravages of Bang's disease is from $50,000,000 to $175,000,000. Not only that, but as I pointed out earlier the disease is a menace to public health. Many hon. members will have read of the death of Edsel Ford. It is reported that he died at Detroit from undulant fever, which is contracted through drinking milk from cows affected with Bang's disease. .
I do not wish to take any more of the time of the committee. We have in this disease the worst known menace to the cattle industry. Certainly it is a subject which should be investigated, and one in connection with which we should do all the research possible. I endorse the suggestion of the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross) and I hope the government will apportion the greatest possible amount of money to bring knowledge to bear on the subject, in an effort to find some workable solution.

When the estimates were first discussed I asked under what item it might be possible for the hon. member for Moose Jaw to offer his proposal, and it was pointed out that the discussion might be had under the item for experimental farms. My interest was aroused after hearing the hon. member on March 17, and I am sure that when he rose to-day we were looking forward to a most interesting speech. I will admit there was some interest in it, and this may yet develop to be a most interesting and profitable afternoon. However, as the leader of the opposition has said, some of us were a little disappointed, because we thought the hon. member would give more details in regard to some questions connected with possible production in western Canada, and that he would outline what has been done in that part of Canada in the last two or three years. I know the hon. member has been fully alive to changes in agricultural production methods, and I believe he has been doing a considerable amount of experimental work. I rather expected, however, that we would hear from the hon. member somewhat more respecting the production of certain cereals, seeds and the like from which oil and its by-products might be produced.

Perhaps he was leaving that for another occasion; perhaps he was rather modest and did not want to boast about what he is doing on his own farm, but I believe he is doing a great deal. I understand that he has nearly five hundred acres of sunflowers this year, and I wish him luck not only in raising the crop but in harvesting it; for I understand that a good deal of his farm is under water at the present time.
Early in the course of his remarks the hon. member quoted from a report showing what has been done in the United States. He also made reference to the fact that agriculture in Canada is very much diversified, so that the farmers of the east have .problems different from those of the west.
I thought the leader of the opposition made a pertinent remark when he said that in all parts of Canada there were farmers who would be successful if they would specialise . in certain lines of agriculture best suited to their district. I know there are farmers in the west to-day who are always a little ahead of their neighbours. My dad always told me, "Boy, it doesn't matter what season of the year it is; always be a week ahead of your neighbour. Start to seed three or four days before you think it is time to seed, and probably you will have your seeding completed while the other fellow is waiting for the ground to dry after a rain." I think if some of the farmers of Ontario had taken that advice this spring they might have been better off.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: Oh, you should have seen the fields.
The hon. member would not know wheat from apples, so that he need not say anything.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: But I know wet ground when I see it.

I think the same thing
applies at harvest time. I know farmers in the west who are always finished their harvesting about a week before their neighbours, who are hauling out their grain when the other fellow is just beginning to harvest his. So that no matter what type of farming you are carrying on it is important to be four or five days or a week ahead of your neighbour; then you will have greater success.
The hon. member went on to deal with certain cereals, seeds and so on. We in the agriculture committee are now considering many of these matters; there are interesting developments in that committee each day, and we are obtaining a great deal of useful

Supply-A gricu Iture
information. Perhaps the minister will not care to repeat some of the information that is being brought out there, but we are getting it in any event. The hon. member went on to say that he was asking for $500,000. He has not moved any amendment to the estimate, and of course we understand that he cannot do so; I think the public got the idea through the press that he could move an amendment, but we know the situation. However, he has told us that he is going to ask the minister to give consideration to his request, and I hope the minister will favourably consider the suggestions advanced by the hon. member. Perhaps during the course of this afternoon we may have a statement from the minister on that point; it would be most interesting. We should be glad to hear how the minister views the proposals advanced by the hon. member for Moose Jaw, and what he proposes to do about them.
I think hon. members will agree that we have had some good men as ministers of agriculture; Martin Burrell, Doctor Tolmie, Doctor Motherwell, Mr. Weir, and the present minister. Each in turn has tried to keep up with the times and has done much to develop agriculture in this country. If some hon. members of this house, instead of going home week-ends, would spend their Saturdays at the experimental farm here, they would obtain a great deal of useful information. Just before Easter I spent a most profitable afternoon at that farm with the hon. member for Moose Jaw. We were well received; we saw some of the experiments that were being carried on with regard to cereals, with regard to production, with regard to early maturing grain, and that sort of thing. We also went through the laboratories. I think the hon. member for Moose Jaw will agree that each of us learned a good deal on that occasion. The next morning at breakfast in the restaurant in this building I suggested to some hon. members that if they knew how many proteins and vitamins were in the bowls of porridge they were eating, they would be pleased, and I said the way to obtain that information was to go out to the experimental farm.
That was just on the side; I was endeavouring to show that all ministers of agriculture have kept abreast of the times and have done a great deal to help agriculture. The work done in developing early maturing wheat has put millions of dollars into the pockets of the farmers of the west, and more millions have been saved by the practical elimination of rust. Those are just some of the things that have been done at the experimental farm here in Ottawa.
I do not know that it is necessary to occupy more of the time of the committee. I am entirely in accord with the suggestion advanced by the hon. member, which I hope will receive the minister's approval. It may not be possible to set aside $500,000 for this purpose right now, but if part of it could be set aside the work could at least be started. I have one further suggestion to offer. I believe that at Brandon, and particularly at Indian Head, in Saskatchewan, we have two of the finest experimental farms in Canada, where excellent work is being done. I would suggest that some of the research work mentioned by the hon. member for Moose Jaw might be undertaken at the farm at Indian Head; it is near the minister's home, and in my constituency, and he is well acquainted with it. So far as soil erosion is concerned it is the best in Canada; we have all the facilities there for carrying on a great deal of the work, and I believe we should take advantage of them. I hope we may hear from the minister before we rise at six o'clock, in order to learn what he proposes to do and how he regards the suggestion advanced by the hon. member for Moose Jaw.
