Mr. Chairman, I should like to take advantage of this opportunity to say a few words. I am sure the committee is indebted to the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross) for bis energy and the research he must have carried on to develop his topic. This topic is commanding wide interest throughout the country and, from the discussion that has taken place, it would seem to be commanding considerable interest in this committee. I am sure the hon. member will be gratified to know that he has finally got the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) to fall in line with the idea he is promoting.
The item now being considered has to do with experimental farms. I am not concerned with, nor have I any definite point of view about the type of research institution that might be set up, but I contend that many research activities can be earned on within our experimental farm system. I think it can be said that the discussion which has taken place this afternoon has not cast any reflection upon the activities of our experimental farm system, it has simply suggested further additions to the work of our farms. Agriculture in Canada owes a great deal to the research work and scientific developments of our experi-nental farm system. I can remember marquis vheat and the contribution it made to the ivealth and prosperity of Canada for a number jf years. That was a result of the research activities of our experimental farms. There is also the work that has been done with respect to rust-resistant wheat. This has taken much of the speculation out of the growing of wheat in western Canada. These and other research activities have been of far-reaching importance to the industry.
These activities are continuing, and they should continue. Further efforts in this regard are needed, particularly with respect to other grains. I think it can be said that some success is being achieved along these lines. There is still room for the development of new varieties. All this work requires institutions of this kind. The hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader) raised an important point with respect to live stock. Here again our experimental farms are in a position to render a wide variety of services in connection with breeding, feeding practices and other promotional work.
The province of Manitoba is fortunate in having tiwo experimental farms. The older farm is at Brandon, but there is another one in
[The Chairman.]
southern Manitoba, at Morden. This is a horticultural farm, and its activities are largely concerned with promoting the production of fruits, vegetables, trees and things of that kind. Just in passing I should like to say a word about our experimental farms in general, based upon what I have seen at the local institution in southern Manitoba. This institution is largely used by the farmers of the surrounding districts. They gather there to see what is going on. I think it can foe said that this institution has done more than anything else in that part of the province to promote the growing of shelter-belts around farm homes, and it has given leadership in the production of small fruits and certain types of vegetables which would not have been undertaken otherwise. It has also done considerable work in the distribution of new varieties. Like other institutions, this one is well staffed with people who can meet the public and who give first-class service to those who go there for information.
Coming back to what the hon. member for Moose Jaw said, I think what he had in mind was to arouse public opinion to the idea that more research is necessary in the interests of agriculture. I am sure he will feel satisfied if he has been successful in arousing public opinion in that regard. If he has arrested the attention of the committee and the country,, he can live in hopes of seeing something come out of the suggestion he has made. I should like to go a step farther in this connection and indicate the direction in which public opinion points. I have a statement here which I wish to read, as follows:
No matter how gloomy the outlook, I never cut one single penny from the budget of our research department. . . . The reason for that is something that any modern industrialist knows and understands. The research of to-day is what will be keeping a soundly managed industry alive and healthy five and ten years in the future.
That statement was made by Mr. Walter P. Chrysler, one of the leading industrialists of the country. I have here an advertisement entitled, "Look up, Mr. Farmer." While I am not particularly interested in promoting the wares of the people who put out this advertisement, I think-
What are their wares?

I am not sure that I know, but I shall refer in a moment to the particular part in which I am interested. The advertisement reads:
And from that alcohol came the rubber for the tires, the explosives in the bomb racks, the plastic for the shatterproof windshields. You

Supply-Agriculture
couldn't point to a square foot of those planes that isn't somehow dependent on high-proof alcohol.
Then in smaller type it states:
Alcohol for war is used in the manufacture of high explosives, synthetic rubber, drugs and medicines, photographic film, lacquers and varnishes, drawing inks, compasses and other navigation instruments, plastics, shatterproof glass and many other products. All of the Seagram plants in Canada and the United States are engaged one hundred per cent in the production of high-proof alcohol for war.
Does my hon. friend intend to table the document from which he is reading?
I shall be glad to send it over to my hon. friend.
I did not ask for that, I asked if my hon. friend was going to table it.

I can table it. I also have a publication which was put out by the Canadian chamber of commerce. The part having to do with domestic markets for farm products reads as follows:
The development of synthetic industrial products, based upon recent advances in chemical knowledge (we refer, particularly, to plastics in this connection), may create a new demand for certain crops, hitherto raised only for food; and so may reduce to some extent the size of our agricultural surpluses.
At least for some years to come, the demand for domestically produced vegetable oils may provide the Canadian farmer with worthwhile opportunities; and it is possible that some of the resulting production (that of the soy bean, for example) may find a permanent place in his programme of cultivation.
I refer to these merely to indicate the trend of public opinion. I obtained some satisfaction in looking back into Hansard of some years ago. At that time I made some reference to this matter, and I should like to refer to one part of my remarks. I quote from page 523 of Hansard of February 1 1939, as follows:
Another thing pointed out was that agriculture in this country was competing not only with the agriculture of other countries, but also with the scientists of other countries. Germany, for instance, is producing from milk casein a material that is a suitable substitute for wool. A large percentage of her clothing both ordinary and high-grade is now being produced from forest products. As illustrative of what industry can do for agriculture, I was fascinated by a statement made by Mr. Henry Ford at the chemurgic conference in 1935. He said he was using in his factory the following agricultural products:	60,000,000 pounds of cotton;
500,000 bushels of corn; 2,500,000 gallons of molasses; 3,200,000 pounds of wool; 1,500,000 square feet of leather; 350,000 pounds of mohair; and an almost unlimited supply of soya beans.
I quote that to indicate some of the activities that have been undertaken. I shall not take the time to refer to other suggestions and observations that were made at that time because reference has already been made to them, to some extent, this afternoon.
As I see the picture, there are two points of view with respect to the need for more agricultural research. First, there is the necessity of providing additional food supplies. From the other point of view there is a need for replacing certain farm products which are not now being produced in the same volume on account of the changes which mechanization has brought about in agriculture. Agriculture, like industry, has become mechanized in this country, and I do not think anyone would take the position that agriculture should not have the advantage of mechanization if it wants it. But agriculture in becoming mechanized has had three things happen to it. In the first place, it has lost what was a potential very substantial horse market. Second1, it has lost a hay and oats market, which was really the power for the production of agricultural products. Third, it has increased its efficiency in production. That being so, I think we should not hesitate for a moment to utilize all our energies in developments that may be undertaken to replace what we have lost through the changes that mechanization has brought about, and if we can by scientific research develop means whereby farm products can be utilized more and more for power purposes in agriculture, it means added farm income for the agriculturists of this country, apart altogether from the food supplies that may be developed from this research work. So that I look at it from the two points of view and I say to the minister that it seems logical that encouragement should be given to developments of that kind.
We have already heard a good deal about the production of alcohol and rubber, and within the last few days we have seen some controversy develop with regard to the costs involved. Surely here is an opportunity to find out the exact position. I fear that too often we look upon wheat as the only cereal from which alcohol may be produced-and wheat of the high-grades costing eighty cents a bushel. I think it is possible to produce alcohol from other grain products than wheat which would change materially the cost picture.
One could go on and say many other things with respect to research activities that may be undertaken, but one hesitates to do so at this stage. I shall simply say, as was mentioned by one hon. member who spoke
Supply-Agriculture

a little earlier this afternoon, that we have had some gratifying results in the agriculture committee in finding out the methods by which some of these activities of the Department of Agriculture were being undertaken. We are finding out at the same time many of the problems of development. All that speaks well for the suggestion brought forward this afternoon by the hon. member for Moose Jaw. At present it looks to me as though public opinion will recognize the necessity for additional research activities particularly in connection with agriculture, and if that is so, I hope that the minister when he brings in his supplementary estimates, or earlier if it is possible for him to do so, will take kindly to the suggestions that have been urged upon him from all sides of the house this afternoon.

I do not think I have very much to add to what has already been said this afternoon. I only wish it had been possible for the hon. member for Moose Jaw to move his motion, because I for one would have been most ready to support it. Many letters have come to me not only from my own part of Saskatchewan but from other areas of that province in support of the idea which the hon. member for Moose Jaw has brought before the committee this afternoon. The opinion which is expressed by some of our western people is that already we are terribly late in our research activities. I know that for some months now I have been in correspondence with the agricultural research laboratory in the United States and have been receiving from them their regular bulletins. If only I had the time to read all the material they send me I would possibly be better informed, but like other hon. members I find it an impossibility to wade through all this very valuable material. I only wish that time permitted me to do it, because then I would be in a far better position to speak about these matters.
The opinion I gather from letters which come to me from Saskatchewan is that there is a fear in the minds of our people that immediately upon the cessation of war we shall find, as a result of the experimentation which has already been carried on in the United States and their valuable research activities, that the markets of this countiy will be flooded by all kinds of new materials which have been made from the various resources of the United States. We are a very similar country to the United States, having the same kind of land and the same kinds of products; and if only we were in a position to develop our own industries-I think more particularly of western Canada, coming

from that part of the country, but without doubt it applies to eastern Canada also-we would be in a position to give employment to our people. I know the problems that confront us in the reconstruction committee in finding employment for our men when they return home, and it seems to me that here in the field of research we have one avenue which we should explore to the very limit. Only the other morning in the agriculture committee Dean Shaw was telling us that they have already started to get the farmers in one particular area to go in for the growing of milkweed. He stated definitely that it was necessary to have these farmers in just one small area where they would be close to the mill which was to be used to extract the juices from which rubber would be produced. I do not know whether Ontario is the only province where this is being done at the present time, but if this plant is as hardy as the Russians say it is-they say it will grow anywhere, in semi-arid regions and up in the far north-we in the west should have an opportunity to develop it.
After all, eastern people have an opportunity of supplying market garden products because they are adjacent to the big cities, whereas we in western Canada cannot rely to any great extent on that kind of production. If a research department were set up, possibly we should receive a more equitable distribution of these newer types of plants which are necessary to industry. The government should have been prepared a year or two ago to have set aside sums of money for *ftiis purpose. I know that in years gone by, in times of peace, when the people of western Canada were asking for money, it was the plea of this government that it did not have the money for the purposes to which our people sought to have it applied. To-day that can no longer be said. We know the government can find money for projects which are essential to the war effort, and I would say that in respect of agricultural research the country's war needs are closely connected with the peace needs which are going to come so closely after.
I suggest that the minister do his very best within the cabinet to have appropriations made for agricultural research, because it promises to provide one of the most important means of keeping our men employed in the years to come.

I believe I can assure the hon. member for Moose Jaw of the support of this group in his presentation this afternoon and his attempt to arouse public opinion with respect to these matters. Of course it is necessary to do more; money for this pwpose

Supply-Agriculture
must be found; and if the hon. member wants to know where to find that money, this group is able to tell him.
I support the hon. member because I am conscious that there is little Canada cannot do if she puts her mind to doing it. I do not wish anything I say to be misconstrued as a criticism of the work which has already been done by the Department of Agriculture in any branch of research, or a reflection upon the national research council as regards any work it has done. I believe these agencies of the government have done an excellent job as far as they have gone. They could do a good deal more if they had what I may term unlimited funds at their disposal.
Personally I am a little alarmed that Canada seems to be behind other nations with regard to scientific research. I do not believe that our young scientists are really given the opportunity to which they are entitled. What happens to our science graduates when they come out of universities? They look around for positions. They flock over to the United States, only because they can get jobs there with bigger pay. That to my mind is not to the credit of Canada. I wonder if the minister is aware, I wonder if the government is aware, that we have doctors of philosophy in some of the sciences working for the government for less pay than a grade three stenographer. That is a fact; it should not be, but it is. When I hear things and know things of that kind I have to ask myself, what sort of Canada are we building? Surely the government cannot escape all responsibility in this very important matter. There is no reason why we should not be one of the leading nations in scientific research, particularly as applied to agriculture. What was it which prior to the war assisted Germany so greatly in making its military preparations? The Germans, not being able to trade in the markets of the world, were forced into the field of synthetics and produced many materials in their laboratories. I believe I read somewhere that more German scientists carried off Nobel prizes than those of any other nation. I have no brief for the Germans; perhaps it was necessity which caused them to do what they did. But when have we produced any outstanding men who have carried off a number of prizes? Doctor Banting is, I realize, one outstanding figure. But we hear of the United States of America being able to do this and that; more recently we have learned of what Russia has been able to achieve in certain fields of research; where does Canada come in? It is true that we have carried off a number of international awards for wheat,
but perhaps that is largely because Providence, with its sunshine and rain, has smiled upon us. It seems to me that our governments act in this regard with the dollar sign stamped on about everything they do. Surely neither this nor any other federal government can escape responsibility for enabling our gifted young men and women to make Canada a first-rate nation in the matter of scientific discovery. There is no reason why this cannot be done. Let us build a Canada worthy of Canadian civilization, a Canada which wall be recognized by the world at large as producing many of the world's greatest scientists. I am absolutely certain it can be done. One thing Canada does not lack is genius; it needs only to be given opportunity.

I believe that support
for the drive which is being started this afternoon will grow, and grow rapidly. I believe, too, that the minister and his advisers will proceed along lines which are sound and proven and hold out hope of being successful. People, particularly in western Canada, are aroused about the possibilities of chemurgy. They hope to make the best possible use of their wheat, their oat hulls, their straw, and all their waste products. Above and beyond this they are looking for further markets for their products, without which their prosperity will not be realized. Surely, in the location of factories or in the distributing of research laboratories, the proximity of the raw product should be the great consideration. Instead of such buildings being erected nearer and nearer to the larger cities, the more remote districts should have the benefit, in these days of easy transportation, of the location and presence of these factories.
I particularly wanted to say a word under this item because I believe that the experimental stations are doing and have still to do a great work in connection with the beef cattle industry. This industry is one of importance. During 1942, 106,741 beef cattle were shipped east to the stock yards and to the feeding lots, and in addition 91,060 were shipped to the United States market. Of course, many thousands were also processed right in western Canada, and in spite of the hardships the ranchers and live stock men have been struggling to meet war demands. The stern and cold winters have developed a type of cattle that are hardy and healthy. Condemnations for tuberculosis in the west have been lower than in any other part of Canada and as low as in any other part of the world. There are still great herds of white-faced Herefords in the ranching districts, and they are of great value, as

Supply-Agriculture

shown by the fact that recently at a bull sale in Calgary one sire sold as high as $2,550.
That great short-grass country which has suffered so much from drought seems to be faced with another season of drought, because the reports indicate that the rainfall this year is very much below normal. Still, that area is an asset to the dominion. Countless thousands of buffalo lived on the grass of those plains in years gone by, They were ruthlessly and wastefully slaughtered by the Indians but about 1881 the real ranching industry had its start. The dominion government then adopted a policy of granting large leases for twenty-one years at the rate of about one cent an acre. Those great areas were unfenced at that time and the ranch homes were widely separated. The struggle against prowling enemies and against the forces of nature, against misfortunes of different kinds, developed men and women who have greatly enriched the traditions of ranching history. I am referring now to a class of people who are rapidly passing off the scene. Nowhere else will you find the same spirit that existed in those days. Stories of cowboys, round-ups, the dreaded stampedes, night-herders and thrilling ranch adventures are stories of the past, because the whole situation as regards the randhing industry has changed. In their day they were noted particularly for their hospitality and no stranger was ever turned away hungry from their doors. Now these large ranches are divided up; they are fenced; the cattle graze mostly on deeded rather than on leased lands, and under the present minister great community pastures have been established and pure-bred sires provided to improve the standard of stock.
The Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act has also made it possible for the farmers to provide thousands of stock-watering reservoirs which have helped greatly in sustaining that ranching industry. There is one ranching experimental station at Manyberries which makes a scientific study of all branches of the industry, and this industry is rapidly becoming more of a science. The breeding, feeding and finishing of cattle require knowledge and care if they are to be at all successful.
At this time I wish to say a word on the need of experimenting not only on the line indicated by hon. members this afternoon but also in the way of making the best possible products that can be turned out for the markets. Although most of the beef cattle are noiw produced by the mixed farmer rather than by the rancher, yet in these great areas they stall live out in the open. The chinook winds

still come and the temperature will rise as much as 50 degrees overnight, so that the grazing areas are exposed and the feeding problem is solved. There is, however, the same determination among these people to produce the best product they can. I appeal to the minister to continue the work of the experimental farms and to nourish this great industry, which is the oldest, and all down through the ages it has been the chief industry of mankind-the tending of flocks and herds.

The proposal of the hon. member for Moose Jaw has been widely and, in my opinion, completely discussed this afternoon, and with great unanimity, so that in rising to support that proposal, I am hesitant about taking up the time of the committee. I shall therefore be very brief.
It seems to me that the matter can be approached from a slightly different angle, and I should like to approach it from the angle of population in the western provinces. We are all aware that there has been a considerable depletion in the man-power of our three western provinces, Saskatchewan particularly and Manitoba next, and we want some day to have these men back. To bring them back, we cannot hope to see them have the openings in agriculture which they had before, because agriculture is becoming more and more mechanized. That process has been going on through the years, and especially in recent years it has been accelerated. Then, of course, the war has taken its toll as it has in other provinces.
I "would mention particularly war industries. War industries have not been given to the western provinces to any great extent. In fact, there has been a great scarcity of them, and the younger men who have not gone to the war, and the older men too, have gone into war industries in the eastern provinces, or what are called the central1 provinces here. It strikes me, therefore, that the best way of getting the eventual return of our population in the west is to get industry in the west. In my opinion that is geared to the proposal of the hon. member for Moose Jaw. We have to get industry, and in order to get industry we have to have research work. I believe research operations are understood at least to some extent by hon. members, some of whom have studied chemistry, others of whom have studied scientific subjects, and possibly a few of whom have done some research work. But while a knowledge of research may be fairly limited, in recent years there has been a great profusion of books on chemurgy, written in a popular manner, and widely read both by the general public and by hon. members. So that,

Supply-Agriculture
despite the fact that all of us do not understand the meaning of chemical formulae, the avenues of research are becoming wider and wider.
The importance of costly research work is emphasized1. The day when the man in the back shop could produce some new invention has almost passed. These problems are approached by teamwork. In that regard I believe the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) might have placed less emphasis on training in this country, because I believe university training in Canada is equal to that of any country in the world of our wealth and size. I am endeavouring to emphasize the point that it is teamwork, coupled with costly research work which is required to lay the basis of industry. We need industry badly in western Canada. Naturally we hear the question : What type of industry do we need most in the west? I would say that first of all the commodity we produce in greatest abundance, and with which we at times have our greatest problems, is wheat. There is no doubt that the uses to which wheat may be put are numerous. One hon. member has told us of the uses to which milk may be put. It is quite possible that there are just as many openings for wheat as there are for milk. Certainly that is a subject which should be thoroughly investigated.	-
There are other commodities which can be grown on the prairies in greater profusion. For instance, I believe potatoes will grow anywhere in the three western provinces. The natural question is, " Then, why do not western people grow more potatoes?" The answer is that there is no market for them-or at least very little market. The only market available is in the vicinity of the large centres, and it is supplied1 by the market gardeners. In the vicinity in which I live, removed only twelve miles from the United States border, no one grows potatoes to any appreciable extent, and there are no large potato growers in the community. But immediately across the border one sees practically nothing but potato fields, and from those fields potatoes by the thousands of carloads are shipped to the Chicago market. I believe potatoes could be grown all through the three western provinces, but until we find some other use for them, something in addition to that offered by the ordinary potato market, they will not be grown.
Flax, likewise, grows very well throughout western Canada. Then there are sections in the west where only oats will grow, and where wheat cannot be grown. Generally speaking, however, the drought areas have found that,
72537-240J
year in and year out, in dry and moist periods, wheat is their best crop. Other crops are gradually coming in from the south, and are being grown in the prairie provinces. In recent years it has been found that two varieties of soya beans are sufficiently hardy to be grown in western Canada, and that production can be carried on profitably in southern Manitoba.
Peas grow satisfactorily in practically all parts of Manitoba and, I believe, in most sections of the other prairie provinces. Cigar tobacco can be grown successfully in southern Manitoba, and as was pointed out by another hon. member, small fruits do well in that area. Then this year for the first time we are growing considerable quantities of soya [DOT]beans, rape seed and sunflower seed along the international border. The fact that these crops are grown introduces the subject of byproducts derived after the process of pressing the seeds. Certainly the possibilities of those by-products should be explored, and I have no doubt experiments are being made in Ottawa. It develops, however, that 'most of these seeds have to be shipped in bulk form to the eastern provinces, and particularly to the Hamilton area, for purposes of extraction. This means that the pulp which remains after the pressing is left in the east, and that the product in its finished form is distributed from this part of Canada. In my opinion those by-products should be investigated, and their possibilities for development in western Canada explored.
Before taking my seat I should like to draw attention to another matter which, although not closely allied to chemistry, has been brought to my attention by a friend who lives in the United States, just across the border-line from where I live. I inquired at the Morden experimental station, and learned that certain farm bulletins had been published on the subject I have in mind. The bulletin I have before me is entitled "Farm Production of Sorgo Sirup." Sorghum is grown to some extent in the southern portions of the western provinces, and certainly it is grown at the Morden experimental station. I learned from correspondence with that station that two varieties have proven very successful, namely, early amber and black amber sorghum. These are .pressed in small plants in the United States, on a community basis and as a farm process. Apparently this type of production has been done successfully, because this 1938 bulletin, No. 1791, from Washington, describes the construction of a small press costing only $788. To-day costs would vary to some extent, but the materials used are not costly, and the
Supply-Agriculture

press could easily be made by any mechanically-minded farmer. I should imagine that under ordinary circumstances the syrup from sorghum could be pressed and used very well indeed. I draw this matter to the attention of the minister, in the belief that a simple process of this kind might well be developed in my district, and would suggest that investigations be carried out with that in mind. May I add that I take much pleasure in supporting the proposal of the hon. member for Moose Jaw.

Mr. Chairman, may I
have the attention of the committee, and lend my small voice in support of the hon. member for Moose Jaw and other hon. members who have spoken in favour of voting a substantial sum of money for scientific research in agriculture. I need not remind hon. members that large industrial concerns have found that if under present day competitive methods they wish to survive, they must spend large sums of money on research. There is no option about that. Competition is so keen that any industry wishing to survive must conduct a certain amount of research. I need not remind hon. members, either, that agriculutre is the largest single industry in Canada, and I do not know of anything of a more constructive or more positive nature that this government could do than to help our farmers to be better farmers, by making available to them that scientific knowledge which will give them leadership not only in the matter of fertilizing crops and choosing the right types of crops, but in regard to eveiy phase of the industry.
I am thinking now of one little branch of agriculture in which my riding is especially interested, namely the raising of fruits and vegetables. The problem of pest control is becoming exceedingly important, and it is expensive to cope with these pests in the production of fruits and vegetables. Therefore I should like to urge as strongly as I can that a substantial sum of money should be voted for the purpose of scientific research to assist agriculture. With the very modest sums at their disposal our experimental farms have done wonderful work, and I should like to pay a well-deserved compliment to the staffs of those farms for that work. In my opinion, however, those experimental farms are not equipped to do the type of research work that has been suggested by the hon. member for Moose Jaw. We need a central organization for that purpose, and I should like to see a central branch charged exclusively with the duty of carrying on scientific research for the benefit of agriculture alone. I should like to see that plant with the most modem

equipment, and I believe the salaries paid should be sufficient to attract the brightest minds in agriculture to-day. I beg the minister not to be too modest in his request. Let us go all-out in this effort, and if we do I am quite sure we shall attract to this work some of the best minds in agriculture and science in this country.

Just about a year ago, Mr. Chairman, Doctor Charles A. A. Stine told an important gathering of chemists in the United States that since 1940 mankind had discovered new continents of matter, and indicated that to-day between ten and one hundred times as much material was available to man as had been available in 1940. Such discoveries as those to which Doctor Stine referred have resulted from appropriations similar to that which the hon. member for Moose Jaw is wisely asking the government to make. I believe the hon. member is entirely right, and I support him completely. I would support him in asking for a much greater appropriation.
There are still great discoveries to be made; we have barely scratched the surface as yet. I believe we can raise the standard of living of all men to a degree not suspected even in the nightmares of men a hundred years ago. We will do this through studies such as the hon. member for Moose Jaw envisages. We will get plenty for the' world, provided we learn how to distribute it. There are many products of nature which up to the present we have not learned to use. It may seem strange, but I have often wondered, I suppose in common with nearly all farmers, whether we could not discover some use to which we might put the weeds that grow so profusely in certain parts of the country and which cost a great deal to destroy. If we could turn them into something profitable and useful, they might not be such a great disadvantage as they are now. I believe everything in nature can be made useful and beautiful if we set ourselves to it.
Mr. MaeINNIS: What about the mosquito?

Yes, even the mosquito. I believe we could use to advantage all our surpluses that are not required by other peoples. At the present time we are fearful of draining our marshes, of establishing new irrigation projects and of putting too many people on the land; we are afraid we may have too much. Certainly that is not a logical attitude for us to take. Such measures as those proposed by the hon. member for Moose Jaw will help us to overcome these difficulties.
Before I resume my seat I believe I should point out once more that we shall have to

Supply-Agriculture
learn how to distribute these goods. If we close our eyes to that problem we shall not be worthy of the position we hold. The time has come when we must have a new scientific method of distribution by which we may enable the people of our own country to buy more of our own products. With respect to the establishment of a plant based upon discoveries resulting from activities such as those suggested by the hon. member for Moose Jaw, the very first question to be asked would be, "Well, where are we going to sell the goods and what kind of prices will we get? Will not the manufacturers of these new kinds of goods bring down the prices of similar goods being manufactured by industries already established, and will not the whole process tend to disorganize the industrial life of the country as it is constituted at the present time?" All such anxieties would disappear if we knew that our people would be enabled to consume the products that might be produced by our industries as a result of activities of this kind.
May I say in closing that I completely favour the proposal of the hon. member for Moose Jaw, and I think in advancing it he has rendered a service to the country.

Since it is just about six o'clock and I do not intend to go on with my estimates this evening I would ask to be permitted to place on Hansard a statement which I had prepared and had intended to read before the close of the discussion this afternoon, if I had been given the opportunity. It merely places on record, as briefly as possible, what has been done in regard to certain matters including dehydration, experiments with soybeans, experiments with the type of dandelion that has been brought here from Russia, and other matters in which hon. members will be interested when they come to discuss this question again. If the committee would permit me to place this statement on record, it would be in print and hon. members would have it in their possession for their consideration.

speechtext: By unanimous consent.

I should like it to go in as a statement by myself. It is as follows:
In view of the inquiries made and opinions expressed by hon. members as to the work done by the experimental farms on agricultural researches of a chemurgic nature, perhaps the following brief statement of work
under way, in which marked contributions have been made to the war effort, might be of interest.
1.	Fruit and vegetable preservation:
(a)	Dehydration. Improved construction of dehydrators and other engineering problems; new methods of preparing material, including blanching, sulphuring, and the like, toward preserving the vitamin content and food values; new processing procedures; new methods of packing, including the gas pack to prevent oxidation and destruction of food values, and the new solid pack method which promises to save tremendously in tin and in transportation; complete study of vitamin content and retention.
(b)	Frozen foods. To save tin and prevent undue wastage.
(c)	Canning. To deal with present problems in tin shortage and including tin substitutes.
(d)	Fruit juices work. In all these, problems continuously arise which involve more research work. For this reason the pilot plant for dehydration research is being constructed at the central experimental farm at the present time.
2.	Fibre production. The mechanizing of the flax industry has made possible the enormous increase in acreage to meet war needs. This increase is from 4,000 to 47,000 acres. In 1943 the British ministry asked for
75,000	acres, which production is quite possible in Canada providing labour is available and at rates of pay comparable to the price of lime fibre and tow.
Aside from the few acres of hemp being grown at the central experimental farm no hemp is being produced in Canada. Further research is needed in an attempt to adapt Canadian-grown hemp to processing on hard fibre machinery; also if sisal supplies continue to disappear some methods of treatment of hemp fibre so that it might be used for binder twine purposes.
3.	Vegetable Oils: Hon. members are fully acquainted with the objective set in the production of vegetable oils in Canada this year and the great need for these, particularly in view of the fact that south American supplies are very difficult to obtain due to shipping conditions and that the Argentine has placed certain embargoes on sunflower seed oil, and possibly others, to the United States, hence indirectly to Canada.
(a)	Flax. It would appear from the estimates of the bureau of statistics that the objective of 2,495,000 acres might almost be reached, although estimates from other sources,
Supply-Agriculture

including the Saskatchewan wheat pool and the Winnipeg Free Press, claim that the bureau of statistics estimates are too high.
It is hoped that a greater use of wilt-resistant varieties and a greater use of Royal, a rust-resistant variety, may be responsible for maintaining the high yield of 1942.
Considerable research as to the use of linseed oil for purposes other than paints, varnishes, linoleums, etc., is progressing in the states and in one or two institutions in Canada. The problem receiving the most attention is the possibility of making an edible oil from linseed oil. The possibility of producing a high-class rubber substitute is also shown by limited researches. Much of this work might well be done by the Department of Agriculture.
(b)	Soybeans. It would appear that the objective of 90,000 acres cannot be reached, but it is hoped that 55,000 acres will be planted. The earlier varieties created by the experimental farms are seeded almost to the limit of seed supplies, particularly the varieties Pagoda and Kabott.
(c)	Sunflowers. All sunflower seed that is available has been sown in the west. Two early varieties, easily harvested, created by the experimental farms (Sunrise and Mennonite) have been sown. It would appear, however, that the seed was capable of covering only some 27,000 acres, which is only one-quarter of the objective.
(d)	Rape seed. Black Argentine annual rape seed to the limit of seed grown by the experimental farms in 1942 and the amounts which could be purchased from the United States has been sown mostly in Manitoba and Saskatchewan and to a lesser extent in Ontario. This was adequate for only some 4,000 acres, whereas the objective was 2,000,000 pounds of oil which would have necessitated 10,000 acres. Researches by the plant breeders in developing pure, high-yielding, high oil content strains, continue.
(e)	Various other oil-bearing plants are still in the experimental stages. These include safflower and mustard. In addition, peppermint oil situation seems to be well in hand and adequate supplies are being produced in Canada.
Again, new hybrid corns in relationship to corn oil and cornstarch are being studied and the values rank high. Starch factories in Canada have used all Canadian corn in 1942.
4.	Kapok substitutes. Milkweed floss and cat-tail floss have been collected by the Department of Agriculture, mostly the science

service's botany division. In the evaluation of these in contrast to kapok the research council has done the work, the Department of Agriculture having no facilities therefor.
5.	Rubber-bearing plants. Thanks to the excellent groundwork of the botany division of the science service, the rubber-bearing qualities of Canadian weeds and plants have been studied for several years. This division also was the first to introduce into Canada the Russian dandelion (taraxacum kok-saghyz).
The Department of Agriculture is covering the experimental and research work in production and evaluation of the dandelion and the native milkweed, while the national research council is studying the industrial use of the rubber produced from these plants.
Experimental farms across Canada have plots of Russian dandelion-seven of the farms having five acres or more 1943 planting.
Commercial studies as to yields, harvesting, and general economy, mechanizing of seed collection and root harvesting, cultural and fertility studies and physiological studies are being conducted.
Milkweed in like manner is being studied in plots on experimental farms across Canada. At the central experimental farm ten acres are planted and are being studied as to mechanizing of pod' harvesting for kapok substitute, harvesting of leaves for rubber, etc. In addition the Department of Munitions and Supply have requested that all seed available be planted this year in order that in 1944 milkweed rubber gum up to the maximum amount -may be available for blending with buna-S. In consequence with financial assistance from munitions and supply, the Department of Agriculture, with the cooperation of the Ontario department of agriculture, is planting 600 acres.
If the product from the 1943 experiments is as useful as now promised, from laboratory studies conducted by the national research council there may be a demand for 15,000 acres in 1944.
6.	Wheat vitamin studies. The cereal division is intensively studying milling methods in order to retain vitamin content of flour in contrast to the British and American methods of re-enforcing white patent flours with chemical vitamins, particularly vitamin B1 as thiamin chloride. Marked success has been achieved to date.
7.	Industrial chemurgy not being undertaken: (1) Plastics. No investigational work is being conducted*of any consequence as to new plastics which might be made from

Supply-Pensions
grains such as soybeans, corn, flax, and others. It is well known that plastics from by-products of sunflower seeds and other materials might be made of great value to war industry and peacetime industry..
(2)	Power alcohol from cereals. No laboratory or pilot plant work is being conducted along these lines. A subcommittee of the national chemurgic committee set up under the Canadian chambers of commerce has had this matter under advisement for three years and a special subcommittee under the chairmanship of Doctor Speakman of the Ontario research foundation, brought in a report in 1941, carefully compiling all available information and based thereon economic calculations with different processes, for example:
(a)	European process-a million-dollar plant .vould absorb 1,800,000 bushels of wheat annually. With wheat at 60 cents, the resulting power alcohol would cost 39-6 cents at the listillery.
(b)	American practice-a three-million dollar clant would absorb 1,900,000 bushels of wheat, md with wheat at 60 cents, the resulting power ilcohol would cost 53-4 cents at the distillery.
The Department of Agriculture, which has representatives on this committee, has also kept in touch with authorities such as N. M. Rosten, an experienced chemist and distiller now in Canada and, formerly from central Europe, who claims the general economic advisability of establishing power alcohol plants to take care of low-grade cereals under war and peace time. This committee has also followed the United States senate subcommittee on agriculture's findings in reference to alcohol from cereals and the possibility of its use in rubber production.
(3)	Synthetic rubber from cereals. No pilot plant has been established nor is work being tone in Canada along this line. It would appear that Mr. Howe has covered this point satisfactorily in his statement to the House of Commons on Wednesday, June 16. What the future may hold as to the price of rubber in relationship to imported supplies and the long-time sources of petroleum in relationship to annual crops which may be grown for the production of power alcohol and rubber, are matters which time no doubt will solve.
The national research council has recently made a careful review of literature and are doing certain biological researches as to a simpler and more rapid method of bacterial fermentation of cereals toward a more economical production of butadiene from cereals.

The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar wanted to ask a question about the scale of wages paid at the experimental farm at Indian Head. It was his information that for seasonal work men were getting twenty-seven cents an hour plus the cost-of-living bonus. Has any consideration been given to increasing those wages?

Consideration has been
given every year to the possibility of doing that. We have made a number of increases during the last five years, but the principal difficulty has been that the farm is employing men in competition with farmers and others in the district. At Indian Head we try to come as closely as we can to the going wages in the area for similar work.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Will the minister explain the terms under which this grant is to be administered?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I shall be very glad to. But first of all I should like to give a brief historical review of the last two years. As hon. members are all aware, the Canadian soldiers' non-pensioned widows' association has been making representations for several years in favour of some pension or allowance for the widows of soldiers who have died since the war, leaving destitute families. A delegation from this association appeared before a committee of this house in 1941 and made very fine representations to the committee, impressing, I think, everyone there. That was on April 3, 1941.
The Canadian Legion made a recommendation on this subject to the same committee on March 28, 1941, and a petition signed by seventy-six members of parliament of all parties in the house was presented to the Prime Minister in regard to this problem.
As hon. members are aware, resolutions have been adopted in connection with this subject by cities, municipal councils, women's institutes and many other types of organizations. The number of these resolutions is very large indeed. I need not elaborate on the various
[The Chairman.]
arguments put forward by the widows' association when they appeared before the committee, because they are well known to all.
The recommendation made by the Canadian Legion to the House of Commons special committee on March 28, 1941, read as follows:
That pending introduction by the government of adequate social legislation, which should include widows and their dependents among its beneficiaries, provision be made by an amendment to the War Veterans' Allowance Act to grant an allowance of $20 per month to:
1.	The indigent widow of a pensioner who is not otherwise provided for;
2.	The indigent widow of a recipient of war veterans' allowance;
3.	The indigent widow of an ex-service man who served in a theatre of actual war.
Providing they have reached the age of 55 or are physically unable to earn a livelihood.
We further recommend that widows in the above classes under the age of 55 years with children to support and not otherwise provided for, receive $40 a month until the children have reached the age of 18.
In May 1942, the dominion convention of the Canadian Legion at Winnipeg adopted a resolution urging a "compassionate allowance" for veterans' widows when they are in necessitous circumstances on the same basis as is provided for widows of men dying on service in the present war under section 11(3) of the Pension Act.
The wording of the petition signed by seventy-six members of parliament of all parties urged:
Such amendments to the Pension Act as will ensure that all widows of deceased veterans of the great war (1914-18) who are now in necessitous circumstances be pensioned in an amount sufficient to provide the reasonable necessities of life.
The special committee on the Pension Act and the War Veterans' Allowance Act in 1941 in its report to the house made the following recommendation:
Consideration should be given to the advisability of extending the provisions of the War Veterans' Allowance Act to:
(a)	Widows of disability pensioners not now provided for.
(b)	Widows of deceased recipients of war veterans' allowance.
It was finally decided that the basic principles involved in the War Veterans' Allowance Act should be adopted as the basis for the proposed allowances.
Ths, War Veterans' Allowance Act applies to members of the forces who served in a theatre of actual war or who were pensioned with respect to their services in the last war. The widows eligible will be those whose husbands' service records can be thus described.

Supply-Pensions
In the case of the War Veterans' Allowance Act, the allowances can be paid when a veteran has reached the age of sixty years, is permanently unemployable, or is incapacitated my mental or physical infirmity from maintaining himself. These conditions will be applied to the widow herself, but the age mentioned will be fifty-five instead of sixty.
Under the War Veterans' Allowance Act, the maximum allowance for an unmarried veteran or widower is S240 a year, with the proviso that only so much of the maximum allowance shall be paid as will bring his total income from all sources to $365 a year. Under the supplementary amendment, however, where there is no other income the allowance may be raised to $300 a year.
These conditions will also apply to the widows' allowances, so that the widow is treated on a parity with the aged or incapacitated veteran.
It was at first intended that administration should be in the hands of the Canadian pension commission. The work of the commission is increasing so rapidly however, due to the casualties of the present war that upon consideration it has been decided to ask the war veterans' allowance board to administer this regulation. The fact that the regulations are similar to those of the War Veterans' Allowance Act means that the board and its staff will have a great deal of experience to guide them in the administration.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is one
of those votes over which there will be no dispute in the house. I am sure that all members of the committee will approve this vote. Many of us, of course, feel that it comes very late. Members on all sides of the house, particularly those who served in the last war, have been pressing for years that some such provision be made for the widows of their comrades who served in that war, so that it is gratifying that now Canada is to give these widows some assistance. But there are several weaknesses which I wish to point out in connection with these provisions that are being made; for example, in the terms under which the widows will become eligible, also the amounts that they are to be paid, and I should like the members of the committee to give careful consideration to these suggestions. I am hopeful that the minister will see fit to make some changes and will not stand firmly on the plan as it has just been announced by him.
In the first place, I think it is a great mistake to make provision for paying money to the widows of these veterans by means of an estimate, because that means that there is no statutory protection for them. It means
that each year a vote will have to be brought in, and there is no assurance that the vote will be brought in each year, no assurance that they will continue to get this assistance. So that I suggest to the minister that either a new act be brought in or an amendment be made to the War Veterans' Allowance Act. That was the intention of the special committee on the Pension Act and the War Veterans' Allowance Act which met in 1941. If the minister will refer to paragraph 10 of the recommendations of that committee, he will find that it reads as follows;
That after further and more complete exploration of the problems involved, consideration be given to the advisability-
And these are the words I wish to emphasize: -of extending the provisions of the War Veterans' Allowance Act. . . .
The paragraph goes on to point out the classes of widows for whose benefit the act should be extended. I ask the minister why that recommendation has not been followed, why it is that, instead of considering an act which would become part of the law of the land, we are merely considering a vote. There may be some good reason for provision being made in that way, but on its face it seems the wrong way to go about the business.
My next suggestion to the minister is that there should be some provision for making the payments retroactive, at least as far back as the date when it was announced that this allowance would be paid. I believe the first announcement was made by the minister in this house on February 4, by way of an interjection in a speech being made at the time by the hon. member for Trinity. The minister will correct me if I am wrong.

The third suggestion I make to-night is that the amount should not be $20 a month with provision for payment of a further $5 where the widow has no income, but that it should be at least $1 a day. I am convinced that that should be the lowest amount we pay to recipients of the war veterans' allowance; that 's, to the men. I think the same is true of the fid age pension. This business of paying twenty or even twenty-five dollars a month under present conditions is not right. People cannot live on that amount of money at the present time. It is out of date, and it is out of line with the scale of payments made in any other part of the British commonwealth and in the United States. I suggest that Canada should pay at least $1 a day, not only to the widows for whom provision is made in the vote, but also to recipients of the war veterans' allowance and to old age pensioners.
Another necessary change is that there should be the right to make some casual earnings, or in other words, the right to earn more than now allowed before the earnings cut down the amount of the allowance. The existing rule has caused a great deal of difficulty with recipients of the war veterans' allowance since the present war. Most of these men could go out and earn small amounts, but they are in this danger, that the money they earn over what would bring them a total, with allowance of $365 a year, causes their war veterans' allowance to be cut down by the amount they earn over $125 a year. This has caused a great deal of discontent, and I think in many cases the restriction has proved unwise.

Another suggestion is that provision be made to give these widows free medical treatment on the same basis as treatment is now given to recipients of the war veterans' allowance who would not be entitled to it by reason of wounds or disability suffered overseas. That would help a great deal, and

Supply-Pensions
I would ask the minister to let us know whether it is possible for some such provision to be made.
I would also suggest that this vote be extended to cover Canadians who served in the imperial forces, and imperials who were domiciled in Canada on or before September 1, 1930, which was the date on which the War Veterans' Allowance Act first came into effect. As the vote now reads, it covers only the widows of those who served in the naval, military or air forces of Canada during the last war. As the minister knows, the War Veterans' Allowance Act itself is much wider than that because it covers any person who was domiciled in Canada before the great war, whether he served in the Canadian or the British army or in any one of the allied armies, and it is only fair that provision should be made for the widows of these men.
Year after year some of us have tried to have the war veterans' allowance extended to cover imperials, those men who served with the British forces in the last war and came to Canada after the war. We have never been able to make headway with that request, but the time has now come when the imperials in Canada should be covered under the War Veterans' Allowance Act, and; a good way to start it would be by protecting their widows under the present vote.
I had intended to suggest that the administration of this vote be left with the war veterans' allowance board, and I am glad that the minister has seen fit to make that change. This board, has always had the confidence of the members of the house to a marked degree, perhaps largely because of the former chairman, Mr. Walter S. Woods, who is sitting before the minister to-night, and I am sure the board will administer this new vote in the same efficient way that they have administered the War Veterans' Allowance Act.
In conclusion, I repeat that it is of the utmost importance that this assistance be put into legislation and made a statute of Canada, so that it will stand no matter what happens here. Governments come and governments go; members of parliament come and members of parliament go; but if this is in the form of a statute there is far more chance of these widows receiving an allowance without any question, and without any difficulties, than if we leave it in the present position of the house having to vote a special item each year.

speechtext: I fear so.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: That does not seem to be fair.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: It would be counted as income, the earnings from that source being steady.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I do not think that is fair, because another woman may be earning $125 for the year from a number of persons, scrubbing or cleaning or helping around the home in some way, and while her earnings may not be steady in the sense that she does not receive them from one employer, nevertheless she may have a number of clients, if you like, who employ her fairly regularly and in that manner she is in receipt of casual earnings which none the less are almost as assured an income as the woman who cleans a school receives. I am thinking of a particular woman when I refer to the cleaning of schools. I agree with the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) that the improvement suggested by the minister is the very minimum of what should be done. I think the minister feels that himself in all probability.
Look around the world and see what is being done. Only this morning I received from New Zealand a summary of their new budget, and it is interesting to look at the improvements they have made at the present time, in the midst of the strain of war. They have improved their old age pensions legislation, the amount being now thirty-two shillings and sixpence a week, and they have made improvements in their veterans' allowance legislation, in their children's allowance, mothers' allowances and so on. When we consider all that, it certainly does put this very rich country to shame, because Canada with its resources is much richer than New Zealand. I wish the minister would give a different definition of the word "casual" in this connection. I am sure there are other members who know of widows of veterans in small towns or in the country who are doing the kind of job I have indicated, cleaning a church or a school and getting five, six, seven or ten dollars a month. They receive it steadily and therefore under this definition they are debarred. Before this is finally settled I hope that the minister will give
Supply-Pensions

further consideration to the definition of "casual", so that people in that position may not be cut off from this very small pension which the government provides.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Is it not a fact that in
almost every case the widow of the veteran would be on a steady job earning a small amount of money? She would not be going from one job to another, so that casual earnings, based upon the principle of the widow taking different jobs all the time, will not help at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: In the case of women it is largely casual. In reply to the bon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), I would remind him that last year when the supplementary allowances were granted to recipients of veteran's allowance, "casual earnings" were stricken out. We were able to overcome that, however, by amendments passed during the Easter recess, and this is of considerable advantage. We are getting over the hard statutory provision of permissive income and supplementing it by $125 as a maximum, and I think it is a fairly good beginning. The essential point is that we cannot go farther. This is a provision ancillary to the Veterans' Allowance Act. My hon. friend said that this is an estimate. It is the intention to try this out to discover flaws and weaknesses in the administration, and then introduce legislation to implement it in statutory form. When I first intended to introduce it I was going to do so by order in council. However, I was informed by the Department of Justice that it would not be the proper way to do it. The proper way would be to put an item in the estimates, and that is why this was done. It will be the intention to discover any weakness there may be in the administration of the provisions, and to introduce an amendment to the War Veterans' Allowance Act.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
What about a widow with
children?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I believe the hon.
member for New Westminster has the floor.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I think the country generally
will receive this legislation with a good deal of satisfaction. Following the remarks of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, I would say that the expression "casual occupation" is one which has caused considerable concern in several parts of Canada. It has to be interpreted in its widest sense. I have had cases drawn to my attention, respecting men who have gone to do some fishing to produce salmon for export to Great Britain. Their earnings
tMr. Coldwell.]
would probably reach $165, and they would be cut off the war veterans' allowance. It was some time before the war veterans' allowance was adjusted.
I join with the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar in asking that the casual earnings clause be widened considerably, and that a little more latitude be allowed, especially at a time when labour is in great demand. I would ask that the line be not drawn too strictly in connection with those who desire to work, and to help out during this time of crisis.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Reference has already been made to the interest of hon. members in this item. As one who has come from the outside recently, I may say that I am particularly conscious of the interest not only of the women affected in the part of the country from which I come, but of the general public. Despite the fact that we are not satisfied with the amount proposed, there will be general satisfaction that at last some move in this direction is being taken. In view of the fact that there is nothing we can do in committee to raise the amount-although that is what some of us would like to do-I shall not take time to discuss that point.
There are, however, one or two other points concerning which some remarks have already been made, upon which I should like to comment. First of all, I would support the suggestion of the hon. member for Vancouver South that the effective date of the payment of this allowance should be made as far back as possible. The hon. member suggested that it go back to the date the propbsal was first announced in the house. I earnestly hope that may be possible. If there are legal reasons why it cannot go back beyond the beginning of the present fiscal year, I should certainly hope that when the minister draws up the regulations-or whoever draws them up-that April 1 might be the date, if indeed it cannot go farther back than that.
I understand the way these things work sometimes is that after the item is passed, the order in council and the regulations are drawn up, and that it is possible that the effective date might be some day next week, after the item is passed. It seems to me that would be most unfair to these women who would lose a month or two through no fault of their own, but simply because we in the House of Commons have taken this length of time to get around to dealing with this item. Surely it is not their fault, and they should not be penalized to the extent of a month or two by virtue of this fact.

Supply-Pensions
The item as it appears in the estimates is an amount of $400,000 for the fiscal year. I assume that amount was calculated with a view as to how much it would take to cover the cases of which the department is aware, and that it was calculated on the basis of a full year of twelve months. I earnestly hope the minister will see to it that the effective date is taken back at least to April 1, and preferably to the date suggested by the hon. member for Vancouver South.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Before the hon. member proceeds to his next point may I say a word on this one, namely, that in connection with making this provision retroactive I doubt very much if I have the authority, or if the government has the authority to do so. I rather fear the effective date will be when the vote passes this committee-to-night I hope. That is why I introduced' it as the first item in my estimates. The regulations were drafted to read from the date of application. The regulations will be announced next Monday, and applications will be invited at once. If possible, I should like to see it made retroactive to April 1, but I doubt if it can be done.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I call the minister's attention to the fact that the amount we are voting is for the entire fiscal year, and that as a matter of fact two-sixths of the amount has already been voted. The minister knows I tried to get him to do something on the basis of that some time ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I did look into that feature of it, because I thought I might be able to act upon this item, once one-sixth was voted. I was informed that because there was a change in the item, not of destination but of construction, I could -not act upon that.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: The only difficulty with respect to the retroactivity of the provision lies in the fact that it is brought in by way of an item in the estimates rather than by legislation. That is the minister's real difficulty as far as retroactivity is concerned. Had he brought it in by way of a statute, as was suggested by the hon. member for Vancouver South, he could have made the statute retroactive, and this would have surmounted his legal difficulty.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: If I had brought it in as a statute, judging from the progress we are making it would not be passed for many months.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
It would not make a great difference, because in that instance the minister could make provision for back pay. 
In this instance not only will there be delay, but widows may be suffering at the same time.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I think the minister is aware of the fact that all hon. members feel it would be unfair to these women if they were to be penalized by -reason of our delay.
I certainly hope the minister will do his best to find ways and means whereby the amount we are voting will be for the full year, dated from April 1.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I might also point out that when the Veterans' Allowance Act was introduced in 1930, and subsequent amendments were made no retroactive provisions were inserted in any of those amendments.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Another point I have in mind relates to the expression "in necessitous circumstances", which appears in the item, and which suggests that considerable significance will attach to the orders in council and the regulations which may be drawn up for the administration of this allowance. One shudders at the way in which the expression "necessitous circumstances" can sometimes be applied. Sometimes it means a rigorous means test which works a hardship unnecessarily. I am sorry the provisions are not contained in some sort of act, so that we could deal with them here. It will be in the power of the minister to suggest regulations and to define "necessitous circumstances". That being so, I hope he will bear out the reputation he has in some quarters for being kind-hearted, and that he will go as far as he can in realizing that these women ought to be entitled to the full amount being provided for them. I -hope he will be very humane when he comes to draft the regulations on that point.
May I say a word or two about the matter of these two sums of $125 of extra income which are allowed. The minister refers to $125 of permissive income, which is characterized as some sort of steady income. Then he says that in addition the recipient of an allowance under this legislation may have another $125 of casual income. As has been pointed out already by previous speakers, one sees immediately how unfair this can be in some cases. On the one hand, a recipient may earn a total of $250 in addition to her allowance; and, because it is casual, because it comes from two or three sources, she is entitled to it. On the other hand, another woman may earn the same amount; but because she receives it from one source, it would be regarded as a steady income, and as a result she would be
Supply-Pensions

penalized. The minister has stated already that we must realize that this is to be ancillary to the War Veterans' Allowance Act. I suggest that this simply increases the strength of the case which many hon. members have been presenting for amendments to the War Veterans' Allowance Act.
Just a few days ago I had a case brought to my attention from the city of Winnipeg, similar to the cases which have been mentioned to-night. This was the case of a recipient of the war veterans' allowance who noted that there was a shortage of man-power and that everyone was asked to pitch in and do his bit in this time of emergency. He answered an advertisement and accepted parttime work as an elevator operator. While he was working his expenses were higher than while not working. In due course it proved to be too much of a strain on his health, and he had to quit the job. Then, lo and behold, he discovered that while he had been working, and spending most of what he was making because of the additional expenses, including extra medical care, he had earned more than he was allowed to receive under the War Veterans' Allowance Act in a twelve month period, so that his allowance was discontinued and he was notified that application for reinstatement would be considered at some future date, I believe in December of this year. Naturally he wonders what he is supposed to do between now and December, and rightly feels that he has -been wronged. I quite understand how the act works; I quite appreciate that we must have regulations; but in the human situations that develop one sees the wrongs that can be created in this way. I am simply suggesting to the minister that all the injustices which existed under the War Veterans' Allowance Act in regard to veterans, and which in themselves needed correction, will be doubled when we bring these widows under the same provisions. Therefore I hope the minister will consider bringing down amendments to the War Veterans' Allowance Act this year to take care of these conditions both with respect to the veterans and to the widows, for whom we are now providing some consideration.
The other matter about which I should like 10 have said a word also has been covered this evening. I hope this provision will become part of the law of this country and that, when it does, the amount will be increased. I was glad to hear the minister say that after a trial period it is his intention to see what can be done by way of legislative enactment. When that time comes-and I hope it will be soon- I trust he will recommend both for the war

veterans and for these widows an amount greater than this $20 a month. It has been pointed out already how hopeless it is for these people to try to live on $20 a month. That has been the situation with our old age pensioners and our war veterans from the time these acts were brought in. Now that we have in some cases the paying of a cost of living bonus, with recognition of the fact that as the cost of living goes up people should be given something extra in order to meet that cost, the whole country has realized that it is unfair to ask a group of our people, such as the old age pensioners and these war veterans, who never should have been asked to live on $20 a month, to continue to live on that small amount. I hope, therefore, that when the minister brings in an act to cover these women and makes the necessary changes with respect to the veterans, he will realize the force of these arguments and this opinion throughout the country and will see to it that the amounts are much greater than we are providing at the present time.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
We in this group are very glad to see that at last recognition has been given to the claim of the widows of the veterans of the last war. I recall that when the pensions committee, I think two years ago, recommended that an allowance be given these widows, the minister or the board took the stand that this could be dealt with only through social legislation, so that I am glad to see that the position has been reconsidered.
I have always felt that if we considered $480 as the right amount to pay a man and his wife under the War Veterans' Allowance Act, then when either the husband or the wife dies, the amount paid to the widow or widower should be more than half that total, because certainly it costs one more than half the amount it costs two to live. There is still the rent of the house to be kept up, for example, and matters of that kind. I realize that this cannot be dealt with at the present time, but I am hoping that when an amendment to the War Veterans' Allowance Act is brought in, consideration will be given to increasing the amount paid to the single member of the family remaining.
I am still not clear as to when the total amount of $490 can be accepted as income. We have $125 as casual income, $125 as regular income, and an allowance of $240. How about a widow living on a small farm. Is anything deducted as rent for the house? I have known the case of a soldier, living on a farm, who had a certain amount deducted as rent for the building. I have known of other cases in

Supply-Pensions
which certain amounts have been deducted for stock, though the income from that stock might be much less than $250.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Are these people recipients of war veterans' allowance?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Yes, and I understand the same legislation will cover payments to the widow.
