Could the minister explain what would be the position of the widow of a soldier living on a very small farm, we will say, where the income is negligible. Perhaps she has to hire all the labour that is required to operate that farm, and by the time she has paid for the labour and paid her taxes, in all probability the revenue will be considerably below $250. Will she still receive the full amount of $240.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: My information is that from the particulars given me by my hon. friend, in that case the widow would be entitled to the maximum allowance available.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Before I offer any suggestions I wish to say that any cases I have brought before the minister or the board have been considered thoroughly and with kindness. But when I have a case that I think is worthy and they do not agree, then I think there should be some changes. I should like to see some leeway given with regard to imperial veterans, and the case I have in mind is that of a young Scotsman who was wounded three times and gassed. He then went through the university and entered his profession. He came to Fort William and was taken ill with lung trouble. I am not a doctor, but I do not think any man can be gassed without his lungs being affected in the future. I took this case up with the pension board and I was advised to go to the British minister. I did so, and I failed in my application. This man has been in a sanatorium for nearly three years and has not received a five-cent piece from the British government.
My suggestion is that the time in which a pensioner must be domiciled in the country should be shortened. My second suggestion is that the pension board should state what this man should receive, and the British government should pay it. Our pension board knows the man's needs better than those who are accustomed to old country ways. I suggest that these imperial veterans who fought in the last war side by side with Canadians should receive more consideration.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
This is the culmination of a struggle lasting many years to rectify a very serious wrong. I realize that it is small
recompense indeed, but I accept it in the light that half a loaf is better than no bread.
I suggest to the minister that the present situation could have been avoided had we had an insurance scheme similar to the armed services insurance provision at present in force in the United States. I bring this up at the present time in an effort to show what is likely to happen after hostilities have ceased. Had we had an insurance scheme there would be no question about subsidiary income. There would be no question, as there is under the present regulations, of a means test in conr nection with extra earnings. These widows of soldiers of the last war are in a better position than they have been, but they must still prove that they are in almost dire penury before they receive any recompense. I suggest that we remember what has gone before and see to it that after this war we do not make the same mistake, and have another group of dependent women who may be up in years and suffering because their breadwinners have died, chiefly from causes attributable to the war. With proper insurance legislation every dependent of those who serve in this war would be secure for the future.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I rise
in order to identify the Progressive Conservative party with the remarks which have been made by those colleagues of mine who have spoken in connection with this matter. This particular item in the estimates of the Department of Pensions and National Health has to do with problems of rehabilitation of the veterans of the last war and, as the hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson) has just suggested, of this war as well. There have been few cases in Canadian public affairs where such pressure has had to be exerted by an organization and others through the years as has been the case in connection with the movement which has finally reached this stage in its development. In many cases such as this a government seems to make a token move-the minister will probably object to my saying that this is a token-to the people involved, but still this is a move in the right direction so far as assisting these women to whom Canada owes so much is concerned.
I repeat the regrets which have been expressed already that the government has not seen fit to bring this about by means of a statute rather than by an experimental estimate. I need not repeat what I said a few moments ago, but there are great difficulties in connection with giving this relief in the way it is being done. With a statute, retroactivity would be possible immediately. The minister has received the opinion of the justice
Supply-Pensions

department and he finds that the question of retroactivity hangs in the balance. I take it from his remarks that he is not very hopeful of the matter being decided in favour of the widows. This is a step in the direction in which many of us have asked the government to move in the past. I suggest that in the time which will elapse between now and next session the minister give careful consideration to the matter of which he spoke a few moments ago and endeavour to incorporate, not only this token movement but a comprehensive and all-embracing scheme into a statute. Then these women to whom we owe so much will be able to feel grateful to this parliament and to this government for making these so-called concessions. I do not, however, regard them' as concessions; they are actually overdue rights. Because they fall into the 'category of overdue rights, an obligation rests upon the government to a greater extent than it otherwise would. We have at least our toe in the door, and I hope the door will finally be opened for those who are so deserving.
This is a general item and I am wondering when it is up again if the minister will permit any further discussion with respect to this matter. There are members of our group, particularly the hon. member for Davenport and the hon. member for Broadview, who have been active in this matter but who are absent from the house on public business this evening, and there will be others in our group who will want to say something on this item.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: There is another item in the estimates on which they can discuss this matter.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I am glad to have the minister's assurance on [DOT] that point because members of this group have taken a very active part in trying to secure pensions for these widows. I know the minister is anxious to get this item through, and I shall be glad to expedite its passage with the reservation I have made and the assurance just now given by the minister.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I had not intended to speak on this item, but in view of suggestions that have been made from various parts of the house that the government is acting in this matter only after a great deal of pressure and suggestions that the government should go much farther than they have gone, I think in fairness to the minister and the government a few points should be brought to the attention of the committee.
IMr. Graydon.]
In 1941 a committee on pensions was set up consisting entirely, I think, of veterans of the last war. They certainly could not be said to be unsympathetic to the interests of the veterans of the last war or of this war. I wish to draw attention to the fact that the government in the action they are taking have gone much farther than any recommendations made by that committee. Those recommendations have already been mentioned. That committee recommended that the government consider the advisability of extending the benefits of the War Veterans' Allowance Act to two classes of widows: widows of pensioners of the last war and, second, widows of recipients of the war veterans' allowance. Pensioners of the last war are men who are suffering from a disability incurred as a result of their service during the war. And who are recipients of the war veterans' allowance? Men who become unable to work and are in necessitous circumstances, but whose disability cannot be proved to be due to war service. Because of the fact that they served in a theatre of war-and that is an important condition-a legal presumption was established that their disability was due to the war. Men who are in receipt of a pension because of war disability were also eligible for the war veterans' allowance. As I say, that pension committee recommended that the government consider the advisability of extending the benefits of the War Veterans' Allowa'nce Act to widows of these two classes of men-the widows of men who are suffering war disabilities and the widows of men who had served in a theatre of war and who were suffering a disability which it was legally presumed was due to the war, although that could not be proved. That is as far as that committee went, after hearing the representations of the organizations which spoke on behalf of the war widows. In fairness to the minister and to the government I think that should be pointed out more clearly than it has been because the minister himself was brief in his remarks.
The minister will correct me if I am wrong, but I take it from the wording of this item that the benefits of the order in council which will be passed are not to be restricted to widows of men who fought in a theatre of war or to widows of men who had a pension, but will apply to the widow of every man who was in the army, the navy or the air force during the last war.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
That is not what the minister said.

Supply-Pensions

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Here is how the amended item reads:
To provide hereby, notwithstanding anything contained in the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act or in any other statute or law, tor the payment out of the consolidated revenue fund, of compassionate allowances awarded by the war veterans' allowance board to widows oi persons who served in the naval, military or air forces of Canada during the war, 1914-1918, who are in necessitous circumstances. . . .
And so forth. The minister will correct me if I am wrong, but my reading of that item is that these benefits are not limited to the classes of people to whom the recommendations of the pensions committee apply. Th'e benefits of the order in council will apply to the widow in necessitous circumstances of every man who is in the army, navy or air force.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: The minister said just the opposite when he made his statement.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Perhaps I did not hear what the minister said, but that is the meaning as I read the item. Be that as it may, the government has gone the full distance recommended by the committee which, as I have said, consisted entirely of veterans of the last war.
I have just one other point to make. I think this item will pass without any opposition because it is a popular move which will commend itself to the members of the house, but I want to join with the hon. member for Vancouver South in his suggestion that this be done by statute rather than by an item in the estimates, but not for the reasons he gave. He suggested that this should be incorporated in a statute in order that it would be permanent. I doubt the wisdom of taking this action by way of an item in the estimates and by order in council, but for a different reason. I am not one of those who have been raising general objections to action by order in council. Those who have raised that objection have been very general in their objections and they have not to my knowledge pointed to many specific instances. I know that especially in war time there is a great deal of action that must be executive action recorded by order in council; but it does seem to me that when we have something that is purely legislative such as this, it would be advisable, instead of taking this action by an item in the estimates and by order in council, to have brought in an amendment to the War Veterans' Allowance Act. It may be that the government has felt that there would be no objection to proceeding in this way and that the quicker and easier way was to put an item in the estimates instead of bringing down a bill and having it go
through its first, second and third readings. But I suggest that the present procedure is a dangerous precedent and I am not much impressed by the suggestion of the minister that this is more or less of an experiment.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I never said that. What I did say was that we would like a fe^v months to discover any flaws there might be in administering this, and that after the experience of a few months we would introduce legislation.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I stand corrected in my statement of the minister s words.
I did not state them quite correctly. The idea is, as he says, that by experience we shall find out what weaknesses there are and shall then be in a better position to enact legislation. But if that principle were to be addpted in connection with all legislation, I do not know where we would land. If something which is purely legislative is to be enacted first by the government by order in council, and an item in the estimates, and then, after people have had the benefit of it for a month or a year, legislation making it permanent is to be brought before the house, I think the method of procedure is objectionable. I know the session has been long and we are very anxious to get through; nevertheless I believe, not for the reason expressed by the hon. member for Vancouver South but for a very different reason, that it is a wrong principle that something which is purely legislative should be decided upon by the cabinet, passed by order in council, and be an item in an estimate, instead of an amendment to the act being brought in.
That was not what I rose to say. I rose to point out that, in taking the action they have taken, the government have gone as far as, and if my interpretation of the amendment is correct, much farther than, any recommendation made by the pension committee. If my reading of the amendment is correct, they have introduced a new principle into the Pension Act. They are establishing a new class of 'beneficiaries, namely the wives of men who served in the armed forces, irrespective of whether their husbands had a war disability or whether they served in a theatre of combat.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
It is now twenty-five years since the armistice of 1918. I think the mark of the greatness of any nation is the manner in which it treats those of its citizens who are unable to take care of themselves, and especially those who are related to the ones who were willing to sacrifice and do all they were asked to do in the war. It is regrettable that it has taken a quarter of a century to bring down what I call token legislation of
Supply-Pensions

this kind, although we are glad that it is here. Yet I cannot understand what logical reason can be given why this grant should be limited to widows of pensionable veterans. Why should not any woman who is the widow of any war veteran be allowed, if she is in necessitous circumstances, to have this grant? Is there any reason? Whj^does this not apply to the widow of any veteran? I should like the minister's answer. If there is a logical answer, I am sure the committee will be glad to have it. I also wish to know, if the figures are here, how many such persons there are in Canada-that is, widows of pensioned veterans, and also widows of veterans-and whether this grant will be sufficient to take care of all those who may make application.
I regret that the administration is to be pretty well by order in council. If the minister has in mind any of the terms of the order in council, I am sure the committee will be glad to hear them. Surely twenty-five years of administration by the Department of Pensions and National Health should enable that department to bring down the proper type of legislative regulation and present it to this house so that hon. members can be assured the law will be administered so as to bring relief to those who have so long deserved it. That the widows of soldiers of the last war should be in need at all is a sad reflection. I do not suppose that any of them are under fifty years of age, so that in a few years they will be eligible for the old age pension and this provision will not apply to them.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: The first question, I understand, was, why was not the legislation applicable to the widows of all those who served. Is that right?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Of course the principle of this estimate is to grant the same privileges to the widows as to the veterans who were eligible for the war veterans' allowance. The principle of service pensions as such has never been admitted in Canada nor, so far as I am aware, in any other country. The provision of the regulations which will follow will be that the word "veteran" will mean in the regulations exactly what the word means in the War Veterans' Allowance Act.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Will that cover the men who served in the British forces?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: The limitations will be exactly the same as they are in the War Veterans' Allowance Act.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Of course the limitation in the War Veterans' Allowance Act is wide enough. I refer to section 2, subsection (j), paragraph (ii):
Any former member of any of His Majesty's forces or of any of the forces of any of His Majesty's allies who was domiciled in Canada at the time at which he joined any such force for the purpose of the war and who served during such war in a theatre of actual war. . . .
It also covers the Canadians who served in the South African war. As I read this vote, neither of these categories is covered.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: In the regulations the word "veteran" will mean exactly what the word "veteran" means as defined in the various subsections of the War Veterans' Allowance Act.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: In other words, a man who served in the imperials will be covered if he had a Canadian domicile?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Yes, if he is eligible under the provisions of War Veterans' Allowance Act. But there was quite a strong public opinion in this country against making the provisions of the act available to imperials who served in a theatre of actual war unless they were previously domiciled here, when such provisions were not available to Canadians who had served in England.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: The minister shall bear in mind that no man who has lived in the mud and passed winters in the snow and the cold can be normal when he resumes his civilian life two, three or four years after enlistment. It is impossible. And because a soldier-and when I say "a soldier" I include the three branches of the armed forces-is considered fit at the time that he is discharged, it is impossible for him to get any superannuation afterwards, because he cannot establish that the cause of his sickness is on account of his military services. This is the answer that I have received hundreds of times. It is not fair, because I know returned men who suffer from rheumatism-

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am sorry, but I must rise to a point of order. My hon. friend is discussing pensions. This has nothing to do with the Pension Act; it is a special allowance under the provisions of the War Veterans' Allowance Act for certain classes of widows. We have in the estimates another item dealing fully with pensions and veterans' allowances.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Well, I will ask the minister not to rise before I have finished explaining my case. I know he is very impatient when I

Supply-Pensions
speak. If he wants me to tell him what I think of his department, I will tell him in very clear language, and I want him to be patient.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Go ahead.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Yes, surely. I want him to be polite. He must remember when everybody was against him I was the first one to speak in his defence.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I am not taking any lessons in politeness from the hon. member for Temiscouata. There is not a more impolite man in the house than the hon. member.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I have no lesson to receive from the minister or from any other minister. And now I fight for the under-dog.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: You should have got your lessons before.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I will ask the hon. member
for Ottawa East to agree with the hon. member for Ottawa South before he interrupts me *when I speak.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: "East" and "West"; there is no "Ottawa South."

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Besides that, the hon.
member for Ottawa East shines more by his silence than when he talks.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Order. The hon.
member must confine himself to the item before the committee.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
We may discuss the
matter in St. Anne's hall before some returned men. I am speaking of men who receive nothing, and I am urging the case of those who depend on the mem. The dependents are not only widows; they may be mothers or children, when the mother is dead, or other relations. In my opinion this item is not large enough, because it does not cover the cases that should be provided for in all humanity.
I have written to the Department of National Defence with regard to one man. The facts of the case are all set out in that letter. This is a poor fellow who was driving a baker's wagon delivering bread. He had only his skin and bones, no flesh, the leanest man I have ever seen on earth, very delicate. He used to drive a wagon and he was called to the army. A doctor's certificate was given showing that his health was exceedingly poor and that he was suffering from hyperchlor-hydria. He was taken into the army, but he suffered all the time. He went into the hospital and received the last rites of the church-

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I rise to a point of order. The item we are discussing relates to widows from the great war, a particular class of persons, and my hon. friend is not making any statement that is germane to the item.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I am submitting that the item is not wide enough. It should be wider and should apply not only to war widows, legitimate or not, but to other persons, the mothers of those in the army and also children.
I believe that the duty of the state is to look after the men who have been suffering by reason of military duty. It is a real shame to think that twenty-five years after the first war we still have a veterans' problem to deal with, and that problem has not yet been solved.
Speaking to the point of order, let me say that my story is not finished. I have two or three sentences to add to this case, and then the minister will realize that I am perfectly in order when I ask that the item should be broadened in order to cover the field I have indicated. Have I not the right as a member of parliament to say that this item is wholly unsatisfactory, that it does not cover cases that are most critical, and that from the human and humane point of view the minister should broaden it to cover at least some essential cases? That is my view, and if I have not the right to say that to-night, we might as well close parliament and all go home, and let the ministers decide what they wish by order in council.
I am speaking as a man who has been offended by the way in which some returned men of the last war, and some men in the army now, have been treated by the army, and I am going to discuss the case of a mother who was deprived of all help because, by false pretences, they succeeded in getting the signature of a young man to his resignation from the army. Telling him that he was getting a pension, by having him sign that paper under false pretences they succeeded in obtaining his resignation, by that action depriving his mother of the allowance to which she was entitled.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
The minister has raised a point of order. The hon. member for Temiscouata must realize that the item under discussion deals with allowances to widows of persons who ' served in the naval, military or air forces of Canada during the war, 1914-18. I think it should be possible, after the statement made by the minister, for the hon. member to stay within the limits of that item. I must follow the rules. Other
Supply-Pensions

opportunities will be afforded for the hon. member to bring up the matter he is now discussing.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I abide by your ruling, Mr. Chairman. I respect the Chair.
Let me now take up the matter of a returned man of the first war. This man was shell-shocked. I have sent that case to the minister. This man receives $40 a month. He can hardly speak. What does he do? He sells cards for ten cents-

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I must rise to a point of order. There is an item in the estimates dealing with pensions for men of the last war, and an appropriation for this war. I submit that the hon. member is out of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: The point of order is well taken. The hon. member for Temiscouata realizes that the matter he is discussing is not relevant to the item before the committee.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I am not going to argue against your ruling, Mr. Chairman, but I will tell you one thing. The minister of pensions has never understood' the rules of the house. However, I will not discuss that case any farther. There are items covering different things; there are items for the veterans of the last war and there are items for the men of this war. Why have we this item before us to-night? Because those two items were not adequate. If they were, why should we have this one? I am arguing that this item is not enough; it does not cover all the cases that should be remedied. I make this statement on behalf not only of the soldiers of my county, but of the soldiers in all parts of Canada, who complain that they are not receiving fair treatment. Is this item only for the female sex? Are we to be told that it is only women who shall enjoy it? In the last war there were very few women except nurses, and what the women received they received through their husband's pay and allowances granted to them. And now we have to fight for these cases, and it is a very hard fight because it is impossible to get any satisfactory answer from the department as it is at present organized.
For a time the board was giving pensions, just the same as the waters flood the fields. To-day conditions are different, and it is hard to get anything. When a man gets a few dollars a month, a meagre pittance, he is considered well off. It affects the condition of the mother; it affects the condition of the children; it affects the condition of the whole family. And it is on behalf of the starving families of many soldiers, and [The Chairman.]
especially on behalf of the classic case of Peter Leclair who wrote to everybody, from the Prime Minister down, seeking redress of his wrongs, that I ask the minister to reconsider that. I say this in the best possible spirit. So long as we are here a society of mutual admiration, making kotows to each other, we shall get nowhere. Soldiers will be most indignant at the way things are going on. How is it we cannot have redress of a wrong on behalf of a poor widow who has been deprived of her rights, when we think of men who get $50 a day for living expenses as dollar-a-year men? And that does not even come before us. There are more allowances for them. We are told it is not under the item. We will take it under the item and wait for it one hour, two hours. I put all these cases before the conscience of the minister and the conscience of my hon. colleagues. It is a shame that in a country like ours we see many soldiers who can hardly walk, who have been shell-shocked, who walk with crutches, who are one-eyed, and who have lost an arm or a leg. We see them in the streets. Sometimes they are begging. The state should have provided work for those who were able-bodied, and should have looked after the returned men who were unfit, whether-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Order. The Chair has some power if he wishes to use it. I have called the hon. member for Temiscouata to order twice, to have him realize that he is not speaking to the item before us. He knows as Chairman of committee I would be the last man to deprive him of the privilege of speaking his mind. But there are some rules which of necessity I must follow. One rule is that in committee of the whole we must necessarily keep to the item we are discussing; otherwise, we would not make headway. I believe I am voicing the sentiment of an overwhelming majority of the members of the committee when I say that we should keep within the item we are discussing; otherwise I shall have to use the powers I have vested in me.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I should like to say another word about the effective date of the payments to be made under the item we are now discussing. I do not feel I can accept as final the word of the minister given a short time ago, when he said he thought there would be no legal power to make payments retroactive to April 1. I wish to say that in putting up a struggle for this point I have no notion that the paying of these widows for the last two or three months will at all make up for what they should have

Supply-Pensions
been receiving over a good many years. It seems to be very niggardly and unfair that these women should have to suffer delay in receiving these payments on account of our delay in reaching this item. I shall call as witness to that point the Prime Minister. Before doing so, however, may I point out that on March 26 the house voted one-sixth supply for the fiscal year commencing April 1, 1943. Then on May 17 we voted another sixth of the year's supply,, which means that at all times we have had supply in the treasury, if I may put it in that way.
On May 18, after we had thus voted four months' supply, I asked on the orders of the day whether it would be possible, in view of the supply which had been voted to begin making these payments. The Minister of Pensions and National Health replied that legal advice had been obtained indicating that this would not be possible. A little later on, by way of further response to my question, the Minister of Finance made this reply, as reported at page 2757 of Hansard:
May I point out that whenever interim supply is asked for the opposition always reserves the right to oppose any item; therefore the granting of interim supply does not carry with it the sanction of any particular item.
I point out to the minister that if there was anything to that right of the opposition to oppose any item, the opposition also has a right to take a positive stand, and we are unanimous in urging him to make these payments retroactive at least to the beginning of the present fiscal year.
I said a moment ago I would call the Prime Minister as my chief witness. I refer hon. members seriously to the debate which took place in the house on April 20 andi 21 with respect to the voting of money for parliamentary assistants to the ministers. Hon. members will recall that at that time we voted $40,000. The matter went through the committee stage and the various readings on April 20 and 21, and finally passed on April 21. That day an hon. member asked the Prime Minister when these salaries of $4,000 a year to the parliamentary assistants would begin. As reported at page 2397, the Prime Minister replied;
The payments will start from the date of the appointments, certainly; but I would say to the committee that some hon. members have been giving a great deal of their time to the work of some of the departments and at a later time, possibly in a supplementary estimate, I may ask that they be given some consideration for the time already spent in that way.
Then, a little later on, on the same day-
The CHAIRMAN; I must direct the attention of the hon. member to the fact that he
cannot quote from speeches during the present session, unless those speeches deal with a problem we are now discussing. I refer him to standing order 41, citation 293 (a):
. . . that a member, while speaking, must not: (a) refer to any debate of the same session on any question not then under discussion.
I would ask the hon. member to observe that rule.
Mr. KNOWLES; I accept your ruling, Mr. Chairman. However, I shall refer to the sentiment then expressed in the same debate by the Prime Minister when he said, in effect, "I am sure hon. members of this house would not want these parliamentary assistants to fail to get consideration for what they have done already, through the failure of this house to get to the appropriate item in the estimates."
Mr. Chairman, I submit that the position is exactly the same in the present instance. Surely hon. members of this house do not want these women to be deprived of $40 or $60 each to which they are entitled, merely through a failure of the house to reach an item in the estimates. If it was possible to make payments on account of $4,000 salaries to parliamentary assistants retroactive to April 1, in addition to their indemnities, even (hough the amounts were not passed in the house until April 21, then although I am not a lawyer I cannot for the life of me see why the same thing cannot be done for these women.
As a matter of fact, there is another reference in the same debate I would have read, had I been in order. However, I shall refer to it only from memory. The Prime Minister said that some of these parliamentary assistants had been giving assistance to the ministers during a period even prior to the commencement of the present fiscal year. He said that at a later date he might ask the house to vote a supplementary estimate to make possible payments on account of salary to those parliamentary assistants for the period, prior to April 1, 1943.
I wish to make it very clear that I am not objecting to the parliamentary assistants receiving pay for the time they worked. I agree with the principle; in fact, we in this group object to the principle that is followed all too often, of having men work for the government for nothing or for a dollar a year. We claim that is the most costly kind of service one can obtain. We accept the principle with respect to these parliamentary assistants; but if it is possible legally to pay these parliamentary assistants for what they did prior to April 1, as I interpreted the Prime Minister's
Supply-Pensions

remarks, then. I impress upon the minister with all the persuasion of which I am capable that I see no reason why the same thing cannot be done for these- widows. I ask him to go to battle on this for all he is worth. It will not make up for what they have been denied for twenty years, but the least we can do now is to see to it that those who are entitled to this pension get it back to April 1.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I may repeat what I said before; apparently I did not impress it upon my hon. friend. I have already taken up the very point which is now in debate. The same idea occurred to me that has occurred to him.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Did the minister take up with the Department of Justice-

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Payments cannot be made until the estimate has been passed by this house. I have explored and am still exploring the question of retroactive payments, and I can tell my hon. friend that if it can be done I shall recommend most strongly that they be paid in that way, but I doubt very much whether I shall be able to do that.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Did the minister take up with the Department of Justice the point I have just raised, namely the retroactive payments to the parliamentary assistants? The Prime Minister said that they would be paid.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: There is an opinion from justice, an opinion from other law officers and an opinion from the chief treasury officer, all to the same effect. I may be able to make such recommendations in future as may overcome some of these objections. Certainly I shall do my best, but I am afraid I may not succeed, so that I want to warn my hon. friend,

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
This extension of the pension to the widows of war veterans is a forward step, and I am sincerely glad that it has been taken. I know personally some of the women who have been trying to bring this about, and even this small amount will be of great help to the women who receive it. I want to urge that it be administered liberally; that is really the main thing I wish to say.
1 hope those who have charge of the administration will remember that this measure is for the benefit of those who are the recipients of it. While there must be investigations, I hope those investigations will be carried out as fairly, courteously and generously as possible. We really need far more trained workers among those who come into contact with the individual pensioners, because sometimes 
the good intent of a measure is largely negatived by the way in which it is carried out. I would _ suggest that quite a number of these administrators should be women, and that if the necessary qualifications can be found in women who have suffered similar losses, they be given consideration above other applicants.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
There are a few points I should like the minister to clarify. I wish to compliment him upon being successful in bringing this matter before the committee at the pres-sent time. I know it has been a battle for twenty-five years on the part of some of the members of this house, and I think the minister has always been sympathetic. I know when the pensions committee considered this matter two years ago there was no difficulty in having the present minister of pensions agree to do what he could in the matter. I think the joker behind the scheme has been the treasury board, and I hope he will be able to persuade them along the lines suggested by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.
The hon. member for Edmonton East very well said a moment ago that the test of any legislation is in its administration, and in that connection there are one or two points I should like to put to the minister now. In the first place I understand that this grant is to be administered in accordance with the provisions of the War Veterans' Allowance Act, and that the widows will be subject to the limitations of that act. I would interpret this to mean that only the widow of a veteran who served in a theatre of war, or a veteran who is receiving a five per cent pension and has attained the age of fifty-five years, will be entitled to this grant. Those limitations will cause a great deal of disappointment to a large number of the widows of veterans of the last war who have been actively carrying on a fight for the last fifteen years at least to bring about that which we have under consideration at the present time. I think the general impression of hon. members is that all widows of veterans who served in the last war and who are in necessitous circumstances will immediately come under this grant, but such is not the situation. As I pointed out a moment ago, it is only the widows of veterans who served in a theatre of war, veterans in receipt of pensions and who have reached the age of fifty-five years.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Or who are incapable or likely to be incapable of earning a livelihood; the same provision as we have in the War Veterans' Allowance Act.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
That is right. I believe the veterans of the last war, who filled premature

Supply-Pensions
graves, who were not able to prove entitlement to pension and who did not come under the provisions of the War Veterans' Allowance Act were the subject of the main fight that has been carried on during the years, and I believe hundreds of widows who are in necessitous circumstances will not be able to benefit under this grant. When this measure was brought in I had hoped that the government was making an appropriation which would apply to widows who were not covered by the War Veterans' Allowance Act, or the Pension Act, because those who came under either of those acts received some measure of protection and some consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Only for twelve months.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
That is right. This provision is serving a useful purpose; there is no doubt about that, but I think it should be extended to include the widows of veterans of the last war who saw service and who for years have been living on the border-line of starvation; not old enough to qualify for old age pensions, in many cases physically incapacitated, with no provision of any kind for their care. I think the minister might still press for administrative latitude, where there are extenuating circumstances, regardless of the provisions of the War Veterans' Allowance Act.
Mention was made of the means test. In my opinion the application of the grant on the basis of necessitous circumstances is much preferable to the meritorious service provision in the old act. Under the old act, unless you were a general and had won the Victoria Cross your widow could never qualify for the grant.
I have associated for a long time with those who administer the Pension Act and the War Veterans' Allowance Act, and I have always found them sympathetic and feel sure that they will apply this provision as it is intended to be applied. A large number of applications have been filed on the basis of meritorious service, and I should like to know if these will be considered, or if new claims will have to be made. I have tried to straighten out many cases under the other section, and I am wondering now if we shall have to go back over the ground and make other applications.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: If eligibility exists under this estimate, the case will be considered.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: There will be a reexamination of the case?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I asked how many
applications had been made and what was the estimated number of applications it was expected would be made.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I do not know how many applications have come in, but the estimate is based upon 1,836 applications for this year.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: How many widows are there in Canada? Are there any statistics on that?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I have not those figures under my hand at the moment. We have the number of widows of pensioners, but I do not think we have the number of widows of veterans.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: How many allowance cases are being paid at the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: A total of 24,192.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: No widows are receiving pensions as yet?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Just an allowance for a period of twelve months after the decease of the recipient.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Has any arrangement
been made to enlarge this grant in case it is not sufficient to cover the number of applications made which may be considered eligible?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: We can always do that by a supplementary. Financial provision will be made for the number who will qualify under the estimate.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: When shall we receive a copy of the regulations under which this will be administered?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: As soon as they are passed. I hope to have them passed next Monday, and they will be tabled the next day.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I	understand that this
legislation will apply to the widows of soldiers who were in reecipt of war veterans' allowance on their death, or who had made application and who would have received it had they lived?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: And who possessed the necesary military qualifications to receive a veterans' allowance.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Assuming that a soldier
was fifty-four years old when he died and was therefore debarred from receiving a war veteran's allowance, would his widow be
Supply-Pensions

eligible for this on the sixtieth anniversary of her husband's birth, provided the circumstances warranted it?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: There is no automatic provision, but I shall be very glad to give that matter consideration.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
If a veteran is a widower
and has a child or children he is entitled to $40 a month instead of $20. Will the same provision apply to widows?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: No.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: In other words, if she has a child or children will she get a double allowance?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: No; there is no provision, but it is a point we can explore further.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: If the War Veterans' Allowance Act is followed, then certainly a widow with a child or children should get $40.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I shall be glad to discuss that further.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Is there any reason why provision should not be made to give free medical treatment to these widows, the same as the recipients of war veterans' allowances get?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: They do not get it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Under class 18.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Only special cases.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: The recipient of a war veterans' allowance gets treatment under special conditions. Is there any reason why the same provision could not be made for the widow?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Of course any veteran is entitled to treatment under class 18, but the endeavour here is to give the same benefits to the widow as were conferred on the recipient under the War Veterans' Allowance Act.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: There is no intention of giving the widow free medical treatment?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: No.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
The minister said a few minutes ago that the widow of any veteran who was covered by the War Veterans' Allowance Act could get this payment. As I read the vote, it refers only to the widows of veterans who served in the war of 1914-18.

I think the minister should make it perfectly clear whether or not the widow of a Soutn African veteran can get this allowance.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: That is certainly the intention, and it will be made clear in the regulations.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I wish to compliment the minister upon the sympathy he has shown to the widows of war veterans by providing this vote in the estimates. These people are deserving, and I should like to see more done for them. I do not think this goes far enough, but it is a step in the right direction.

Amendment agreed to.
Item as amended agreed to.
21/0. Departmental administration, $730,858.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few remarks on the subject and give a general idea of the financial position of the department. In presenting the estimates of the Post Office Department for a period overlapping the fourth and fifth years of the war, I have to report that this service is continuing to the best of its ability to carry out its obligations to the public and its cooperation with other government bodies referred1 to in the statement which I made to the committee in July last. I have no desire to occupy time unnecessarily by again going over the ground traversed on that occasion, but it may not be out of place to point out that this cooperation has kept pace with the expansion of functions and activities, such as rationing, which has taken place during the past year.
Taking up first the financial position of the department as shown by revenue and expenditure, may I point out that in presenting the post office estimates last year I was able to report receipts for 1941-42 which up to then constituted an all-time high for the department. For 1942-43 the report is the same. The gross revenue shows an increase of $3,697,979 over 1941-42, or 6-6 per cent. The net revenue increased by $2,874,890, or 6'24 per cent. Increase in revenue merely reflects increased mailings. The increase mentioned does not indicate the extent of increased mailings, because it is necessary to consider also the postage value of franked mail which in 1942-43 showed an increase of more than $700,000 over 1941-42. Augmented mail volume necessitates added operational costs- more staff, more salaries and bonus, more space in railway cars, on planes other than T.C.A. and on steamboats, and more expenditure for stationery and equipment of all kinds.

Supply-Post Office
If we now look at expenditure figures for a moment we find that there is an increase over
1941-	42 of $3,240,118, or 12-8 per cent, and I wish to call the attention of the committee to the differing conditions in the two years under review.
The first point of difference is in the cost of living bonus. In the months of April, May, June, and July of 1941, straight salaries only were paid. Commencing August 1, employees under $2,100 per annum received the benefit of an 11 per cent cost of living bonus.
In 1942-43, the cost of living bonus was operative throughout the whole year, 11 per cent being the rate from April to July inclusive and 17 per cent for the remaining eight months.
So that in comparing the two years it is necessary to take into account the fact that during the first four months of 1942-43 an 11 per cent bonus was paid, whereas during the same period of 1941-42 there was no bonus, and that during the remaining eight months of 1942-43 the bonus rate was 54-5 per cent higher than during the same period of 1941-42.
Translated into figures, the bonus payments in 1941-42 amounted to $1,039,369, while in
1942-	43 they were, almost $2,105,000. Even if there had been no increase in the bonus rate, the expenditure under this heading in 1942-43 would still have been approximately $500,000 greater than in 1941-42.
The second point of difference is the increased volume of mail. Expenditure from the railway mail service vote alone in 1942-43 shows an increase of nearly $600,000 over 1941-42. A large part of this increase is in mail service by railway, but a greater part is in mail service by steamboat. As explained last year, ocean conveyance has been wholly provided for by the Post Office Department since subsidies were withdrawn by the Department of Trade and Commerce. Seaborne mail now consists largely of letters and parcels to troops overseas and letters from them to relatives and friends here.
To illustrate the situation more clearly, may I point out that prior to the war post office estimates provided to the extent of only about $325,000 for mail service by water. Hon. mem-oers will note that the estimates for 1943-44 contain provision to the extent of $2,500,000.
A third point of difference is in mail service ay air and by ordinary land conveyance. The expenditure from this vote in 1942-43 was $988,000 greater than in 1941-42. This is due to two factors, first the expansion of Trans-Canada and other air services to meet the needs of the public and war conditions, and
second, rising costs of service by ordinary land. These are factors over which the department has no control and which must be provided for if service is to be maintained.
The estimates for 1943-44 show an increase of slightly over $3,000,000 as compared with 1942-43. On examination it will be found that this increase is very largely due to the categories of expenditure I have already mentioned, namely, cost of living bonus, mail service by railway and steamboat, also mail service by air and ordinary land conveyance.
With the exception of these items the estimates for this year are practically on a level with those of the preceding fiscal period.
In conclusion, I wish to pay tribute to the loyalty and' cooperation of all postal personnel under frequently trying war-time conditions. Postal workers, whether they be paid from parliamentary appropriation, postmasters of revenue offices and their assistants, mail contractors and their couriers, are all contributing to the support of our country's war-time financing, and many of them are giving of their spare time in war activities of various kinds. I am glad indeed to take advantage of this opportunity to express on behalf of the government appreciation of the services rendered by postal personnel, whether acting in their official capacities or as private citizens of this dominion.

I wish to congratulate the minister upon the statement he has just made and to associate myself with the tribute of appreciation he has paid to the members of the post office staff right across this country for performing such valuable services in our national life under very trying conditions. I think it is remarkable that the Post Office Department has been able to give the service it has been giving to the people of Canada and to our armed forces scattered over the entire world with so very few complaints.
I have a suggestion I wish to make in the hope that consideration will be given to it by the minister between now and next year. Of course, we always have to speak in terms of improving these services. It amazes me that the Post Office Department is able to give as good a service as it does with political patronage as it is in this country. I should like the minister to bring in a recommendation while he holds office to set up a public service utility to administer the handling of mail along the lines of the operation of the Canadian National Railways, removing the service entirely from political patronage. I say this as a member of the opposition, expressing a good deal of sympathy for members of the govern-
Supply-Post Office

ment when I read some of the sessional papers and realize how embarrassed the members must be when they recommend the appointments that some of them do, and then have the grief that frequently follows.
I have here a sessional paper in connection with the appointment of a postmaster at Endeavour, in my constituency. I would not take the time to discuss it if it were not a typical case.
Perhaps the hon. member would not mind waiting until we reach the next item, 241, which deals with post offices. The item before us deals with the general administration of the department.

I was going to cite
this case to support my argument but if it will accommodate the minister I shall be glad to resume my remarks when we reach the next item.
Thank you.

I understand that the
Post Office Department handles the registration cards. When these forms are sent out to the individual post offices, what is the machinery for registering the people? Are they counted or numbered?
The names are registered through to the local registrar of the district concerned.

Suppose a post office
gets 100 or 150 of these forms. Does each individual postmaster have to account for each one of those forms? They are not numbered yet, are they?
My officials advise me that the postmasters have to account for every form.
The minister has referred to the increase in revenue, both gross and net. Would he indicate what sum he anticipates receiving from the extra cent postage, dividing it between land and air?

It is a little early to give any definite information, but it would seem that about $9 millions is indicated at the present time from the one-cent revenue tax placed by the Department of Finance on the post office.
Including both land and air?
Yes, all letters.
Can he divide it? He is not in a position to say what portion of that will be derived from the seven cents for the air letters?
Not as yet, no.

Could the minister give
any general statement with regard to the condition of airmail overseas? Is it received at present at both ends, and if it is, can he give any explanation of the extraordinary delays which occur, particularly in the mail coming westbound?

Yes, I think I can give the hon. member that information. Notices are being sent to ithe postmasters throughout this country that, commencing immediately, we shall be in a position to take care of the 30-cent half-ounce letter, namely, the ordinary letter which can be handled by air from now on to Britain. Outside of an accumulation on account of very, very heavy mailings of the armed forces letters at Christmas time, there have been very few delays except the ordinary delays which cannot be avoided owing to bad flying weather. I know my hon. friend understands that there have been no delays in -the airgraphs. While we are on the point of airgraphs, I might say that we have been able to speed this service up considerably. At first the messages had to be dispatched to the United States, either New York or Rochester for processing. The Canadian airgraph messages received the same treatment in proportion to the number of United States airgraph messages, which they call "V mail." If a very heavy United States mail arrived, there would be delay in getting some of our airgraph messages processed, and considerable delay did occur. I am glad to be able to report to the committee that that work is now being carried- on in Canada and will certainly cut the time by at least forty-eight hours, and in many cases, such as delays on account of heavy United States mailings, a great deal more than that.
That relates to mail going to Britain. I would advise the hon. member, although I think he knows, that the Post Office Department of this country is not responsible for mails until they arrive in Canada. We are not responsible for mail dispatched from Britain; that is the responsibility of the Postmaster General of Great Britain. We are no more responsible for them than we are for mail sent from Mexico or any other part of the world. I know they are having trouble. I think I can say, without giving away any confidences-it is, perhaps, clear to everyone-that there are more planes going to Britain than are returning. That is the

Supply-Post Office
story. It is easier to get mail across whereas the Postmaster General of Great Britain at times finds difficulty in- obtaining enough planes to handle all the airmail which is destined for Canada and the United States. There is a considerable accumulation of airmail for Canada. The Right Hon. Mr. Morrison, then Postmaster General of Great Britain, discussed the matter with me when I was in England last year, and explained the difficulty. There was just not a sufficient supply of planes to take care of the airmail, and rather than delay it all the way down the line and hold back further airmail which was coming in, he dispatched a very large amount of it on a fast ship to Canada and so cleaned up the accumulation. Had it not been done in that way there would have been delay for months and months before the accumulation could have been disposed of.
Can I gather from what the minister has said that the westbound airmail for some time has been coming by direct plane and not by a more devious route?

I think I can say that it
has been, coming direct for some time.

Would the minister give us a little more detail with respect to the revenues that have been received? I should like a break-down of the revenues which are produced:. How much do we receive, for instance, as a result of overseas mail, of first-class mail, and of second-class mail? I appreciate the difficulty of answering the question in respect to the extra cent tax. We must, however, be receiving quite a revenue from first-class mail, with the rate of four cents on every letter which is posted.
I can give my hon. friend the information for the year previous but I cannot give it ito him yet for the last year. It will be available in a few months.

If the minister can give it for the year previous it will help to some extent, but we are getting well on in the year and it would seem to me that a balance could be struck. However, I know we can call for a return at any time. Will the minister give us the latest he has?

I will give the poundage
and the revenue: First-class, 22,000,000 pounds, revenue $26,000,000; second-class, 116,420,000 pounds, revenue $1,853,600; third-class, 33,700,000 pounds, revenue $4,500,000; parcels, 77,000,000 pounds, revenue $6,500,000; local letters, revenue $5,100,000.
Has the minister the overseas amount? Are the figures separated?

I can give it in pounds, if that will help the hon. member. I have that information here for the last three calendar years. Letters and postcards: 1940, 124,005 pounds; 1941, 275,268 pounds; 1942, 502,909 pounds. Other classes except parcel post: 1940, 569,665 pounds; 1941, 1,307,797 pounds; 1942, 1.975,698 pounds. Parcel post: 1940, 3,953,260 pounds; 1941, 6,470,089 pounds; 1942, 15,806,645 pounds. Tobacco parcels: 1940, not available; 1941, 2,506,606 pounds; 1942, 4,643,375 pounds. Totals: for the calendar year 1940, 4,646,930; 1941, 10,559,760; 1942, 22,928,627 pounds.

I thank the minister for the information, and now that I have these figures I am not so certain what to do with them. I was more anxious to get a break-down of revenue than of poundage. The minister said that there were more planes going eastward than coming from overseas. Is that on account of the feriy command, the bombers going overseas?
Yes.
In connection with the congestion of mail that might result, coming from overseas, is there a priority in the carriage of mail?

The hon. member no doubt heard the statement of the Minister of Munitions and Supply with regard to the new Canadian service. That, as I understand it, is for the armed services and official mail and not for civilian use. I understand that is the tenor of the agreement. So far as we are concerned, in our mail going to Britain the first priority is airgraph. In airgraph we can move a tremendous number of messages in case of congestion. We can get more letters over and have a faster communication than in any other way. Next comes the armed forces' air letter. That is much lighter material or paper than is ordinarily used, and that is second priority. Letters to troops go first so far as we are concerned, but of course there are exceptions. If there were some urgently required government dispatches or something of that kind that would be an exception. There must be exceptions to every rule.

I do not know whether the question I am about to ask is pertinent to this item. With regard to the operation of the Post Office Department, there must be some working relationship with the board of censors, because a good deal of censorship is complicated with the mail service and the
Supply-Post Office

Post Office Department generally, I think it would be of interest to the committee if the Postmaster General would indicate the manner in which the two services, that of censorship and the Post Office Department, actually operate in a mechanical way. I would ask him also if the arrangements between the board of censors and the Post Office Department are working satisfactorily.

I appreciate the interest the leader of the opposition has in this matter, and I can assure him that my officials and those of the war services are getting on very well. In fact, a large number of them, engaged in postal censorship, were formerly postal employees on the payroll of the Post Office Department until a few months ago. I do not want to go into details because I am not dealing with that matter, but if the censors ask the Post Office Department for requirements we try to cooperate and see that they get them. That is about as much as I can say. Censorship does not come under my department.

I was not suggesting that it did. But I did want to know something of the relationship that exists between the two branches. Perhaps it would help the minister in giving the details if he could tell me what is the mechanical arrangement in connection with the submission of letters and other documents that go through the post office. Are there representatives of the board of censors in the Post Office Department, or how is the censorship actually worked out mechanically?
There is a post office and a dead letter office in the censorship.

What the minister means may be perfectly clear to him; but does that mean that, so far as letters that go through the ordinary mail are concerned, a proportion of them are censored, or how is the censorship actually worked with regard to the great volume of mail? I can understand that all letters are not opened, but a certain percentage of them are opened from time to time and I should like to know whether any letters are opened that are posted in Ottawa for instance. Are there any opened and examined by the censor? If so, which letters does the censor actually choose for examination out of the great volume of mail, and how is it actually done, having relation to the position of the Postmaster General?
I have no information.

The Postmaster General is leaving the matter surrounded by an air of mystery. When I first asked the question I did so innocently because I did not know that

there was any mystery surrounding it. Surely the Postmaster General is in a position to give a simple answer to my question. Are there representatives of the board of censors in any branch of the Post Office Department?
No.

Can the minister explain this:	I receive letters from Great Britain
which reach me through the machinery of the post office. A very considerable number of them, almost all of them, are opened, and fastened up again with a white strip of paper having black lettering on it. Is that done in Great Britain, or in Canada?
In Great Britain.

Is anything similar to
that done after a letter has been put into the hands of the officials of the Postmaster General in Canada for dispatch to Great Britain?

That is really a question
for the Department of National War Services. The matter of censorship is under the minister of that department. I know when it was under the post office I learned, when talking to officials from Great Britain, that they were not very keen on information being given; in fact they impressed strongly upon officials of this department and upon myself that we should not give information with respect to the details of the system of censorship. I would rather have the Minister of National War Services deal with this matter, because it comes under his jurisdiction, and he will know the general feeling, particularly in Great Britain and the United States, with regard to censorship. I believe they work along nearly the same lines.
That is good enough for me.

Perhaps the minister might have said that he declined to answer my original question for purposes of security rather than the answer he actually gave. My understanding is that the board of censors has representatives in some of the post offices.

Our employees have to
do the physical act, if that is what the leader of the opposition means. They must perform the physical act of moving the mail to the censor; to that extent the hon. member is correct.

For the time being I
believe that clears up what I wanted to know, namely, the relationship between the board of censors and the Post Office Department. It seemed to me that from the point of view

Supply-Post Office
of mechanics the two departments would have to work closely together, hand in hand, in* order that censorship might be carried out. Naturally the details of censorship would not fall within the purview of the minister's department, but rather within the department headed by the Minister of National War Services. I did want to know what degree of cooperation existed between the two departments.
Mr. LaFLECHE:	I take it the leader of
the opposition inquired as to the mechanics of dealing with the situation. If I might be permitted, I would say that on the staff of the censorship branch there are two senior employees from the Post Office Department occupying top positions, and they see to all the requirements, including those I am sure in the mind of the leader of the opposition. I shall take note of what has been asked tonight, and at a later time I shall give as much detail as I can.

I believe that answers
one of the questions I had in mind. It seemed to me there must be some liaison of some description between the Post Office Department and the department of the minister who has just taken his seat.

If I did not make it clear before, may I tell the leader of the opposition that a considerable number of our employees are on loan to the Department of National War Services. These are experienced men, lifelong employees of the department.

Are those employees
seconded from the Post Office Department to the Department of National War Services? Do they now come within the jurisdiction of the Department of National War Services, so that they are no longer connected with the Post Office Department?

That is correct, for the
duration of the war, while they are retained in the Department of National War Services.
How many officials have been seconded from the Post Office Department to the Department of National War Services?

Twenty employees. Does
the leader of the opposition want the names?
No.

The minister said censorship from Great Britain to Canada was done by British authorities. With respect to mail going the other way, namely from Canada to Great Britain, is it done by Canadian authorities?
Yes.

While this item is before the committee I should like to say only a few words. I do not believe one letter of my Canadian mail has been opened by any censor; I refer to any letter written to me in Canada. But, while I make that statement, I must protest against any mail addressed to any member of parliament being opened by anyone-a censor, or anyone else. The basis upon which I make that objection is simply this: A member of parliament is elected by his people. Those people had absolute confidence in him, or he would not have been elected.

The majority of them
had, you mean.

I would draw the hon.
member's attention to the fact that censorship is under the Department of National War Services.

All right; I shall take it
up when the estimates for that department are before the committee. I send this envelope to the Postmaster General, and I want him to tell me by whom it was censored. It is addressed to "E. G. Hansell, M.P., House of Commons, 'Ottawa, Ontario."
Where is it from?
England.
My officials advise me this was censored in England.

Then let me have it
back, please. I was going to add that that letter was from my mother. I receive from her letters every few weeks. I have never had a letter from her since the war started which has not been censored-not one.

Item agreed to.
241. Post offices, including salaries and other expenses of headquarters and staff post offices and supplies and equipment for revenue post offices, $18,475,433.

A few minutes ago I
mentioned a case which I am afraid is fairly typical. This is about the fourth of its kind brought to my attention in my own constituency. While Endeavour is not a very large place-possibly very few hon. members have ever heard of it-the people who live there are just as important in the life of Canada as the people who live at Ottawa, Toronto or Montreal. Those people make their full contribution in war time as in peace time. Unfortunately the majority of them are not permitted to travel across Canada to learn what contribution Canada
Supply-Post Office

is making in the present conflict. They are able to judge what we do with our money by our administration of post offices.
This is the case of a postmaster who in April, 1942, was found to be $386 short in funds when the inspector came to check the cash. He signed a statement to that effect. This is the statement:
I hereby acknowledge that the sum of $386 of post office funds has not been accounted for by me as required by statute.
I am sure that, in failing to produce these funds, I have rendered myself liable to prosecution and to such other action as the Postmaster General may find it necessary to take, in order to protect the public interest.
Is that a sessional paper?

Yes, a sessional paper which was brought down on February 10. In due course I want the Postmaster General to state what has been done about this man who admits that he is liable to prosecution when he is short public funds to the extent of $386. The inspector did what an inspector should do in a situation like this; he canvassed the field, selected an ex-service man and appointed him as temporary postmaster. The wife of this ex-service man is a graduate of Queen's university, and she was to be assistant postmaster. In due course the inspector advised Ottawa and Ottawa advised the defeated Liberal candidate in that riding, telling him what had happened and asking him what to do about it. That was on April 27.
Perhaps the hon. gentleman means that he was asked for recommendations, not for instructions.

I will read the letter if
the minister wishes. In any event Mr. Barrie, who was the defeated candidate, replied:
After having given the matter of filling the vacancy at Endeavour, Saskatchewan, full consideration, I am attaching hereto the nomination in favour of Nelson R. McGregor.
Then he goes on to give Mr. McGregor's qualifications, and this gentleman was appointed on August 8. The people of the community were kept in suspense from April until August, but then the local Liberal association got together and wrote a letter to the district superintendent, as follows:
We kindly ask you to hold us abeyance the appointment of the postmaster at Endeavour and the appointment of Mr. McGregor. We, as association, recognize that Mr. McGregor is not a residence of Endeavour and do not wish him to succeed Mr. Izdebski as postmaster. We are taking this matter up with the Postmaster General at Ottawa.
