I am reading this letter as it appears in the official file. Then they passed some resolutions, copies of which were sent to the Postmaster General. It was moved:
That we recommend Mr. Oscar Clementson to succeed former postmaster Mr. Bolas Izdebski.
Another motion was:
That the committee wait for Mr. Ross Barry to discuss the matter for Mr. Clementson about the post office.
Another motion was that Mr. Starkes arrange to meet Mr. Ross Barrie; another motion was that the committee circulate a petition for the appointment of Mr. Oscar Clementson as postmaster. Those resolutions were passed on August 14. Eventually Mr. McGregor, who was appointed, wrote to Mr. Underwood1 on August 22 saying:
Through unavoidable circumstances arriving since I had made my application as postmaster, I am unable to accept the position.
Then the Post Office Department went to a great deal of trouble. Mr. Hunter, the district superintendent in Saskatoon, who is a very efficient man, was put to the expense and trouble of telephoning long distance to see whether Mr. McGregor was taking the office or just what was going to happen. Then it was necessary for Mr. Underwood to write Mr. Barrie again on August 28 telling him of the trouble and of all the. applications that had been received. Finally Mr. Clementson was appointed, about August 31. Then on September 26, after a good deal of local trouble, Mr. Clementson declined the position and on October 8 Mr. Avery found it necessary to write Mr. Barrie regarding the situation.
Who represents the constituency now?

I happen to be the member. I want to make it perfectly clear that when I am sitting across the floor of the house as a member of the government we shall not have this sort of thing in the administration of the affairs of the Post Office Department in this country.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: What would you recommend now?

I shall come to that in a few moments. A short time ago I said we should set up a public service commission to administer the affairs of the Post Office Department, so that the hon. member for Essex East, for example, would be relieved of the embarrassment which I am sure he has felt when he has had to recommend one person for appointment and thus antagonize a great

Supply-Post Office
many others. Now here is a personal letter from Mr. Barrie, but since it appears in this file I presume it becomes public. He says:
This office has been very unfortunate in that I have now nominated two returned men for the position and each have for personal reasons and certain circumstances refused the appointment.
He does not want to make another recommendation. The man who was selected by the inspector in April, had been carrying on throughout the summer without a single complaint; he was a returned soldier, but for some reason which Mr. Barrie does not give here Mr. Sinclair was not appointed. Then on October 15 Mr. Avery wrote a long letter to Mr. Barrie, outlining the situation and saying:
Mr. Sinclair is a returned soldier who saw service in England, in France and in Belgium during the last war. He has conducted the post office satisfactorily from the 17th April,
1942.	He first asked to be relieved of the office on the 31st August, but as the person nominated by you declined it was necessary to ask Mr. Sinclair to carry on for a further period. He again asked definitely to be relieved of the office on the 30th September and again your nominee declined and Mr. Sinclair is still carrying on.
On October 30 Mr. Barrie wrote another letter, in which he said:
I regret that this matter has been so long delayed and then has to end in this manner but it was unavoidable. I trust that this will allow you to settle this matter at least for the time being, if not permanently.
Then the local branch of the legion found it necessary, on November 27, to send a telegram to the Postmaster General, as follows:
Present postmaster Sinclair appointment be sustained request of executive committee.
So that Mr. Sinclair, the man who was selected in the first place, finally was appointed on December 18. On January 7, 1943, Mr. Underwood wrote Mr. Barrie as follows:
Mr. Dugald Patrick Sinclair, returned soldier, was appointed pennanently as postmaster at the above office dating from the 18th December.
May I ask what was the date of the last letter the hon. gentleman read? That would not be during the war-time period, would it?

It was dated January 7,
1943.	The correspondence goes back to April 17, 1942. The point I wish to make is that in this community where there were veterans of the last war residing, we see this state of confusion; we see public funds unaccounted for, and no satisfactory investigation carried on. Two men are recommended), for political reasons, and appointed; their appointments are unsatisfactory to the people of the community, and finally the man selected by the
inspector in the first place was appointed. I want to urge, Mr. Chairman, that the present Postmaster General give consideration to removing the Post Office Department from the embarrassment and the waste of time and energy entailed in having to write airmail letters and send communications to defeated Liberal candidates before an appointment can be made to a little country post office. I should like the Postmaster General to tell me now what is his policy in connection with cases like this of the former postmaster at Endeavour, who was short 8386. I understand that if a postal clerk here in the city post office is caught to-night taking an envelope with a dollar bill in it, he is liable to a very heavy penalty. It appears, however, that if the individual concerned is the postmaster and takes something over $300, nothing very much happens to him. Will the minister tell me what happened in connection with this defalcation and make some comment on my suggestion as to the possibility of removing these appointments from political patronage?
From what the hon. member has said I would judge that all the persons concerned with this appointment were returned soldiers.
That is right.
I would judge also from the statements the hon. member has read that it would be a purely departmental matter.
No.
I do not think it was referred to me.
The minister received a telegram.

I received a telegram from the legion. I think it is purely a departmental matter and I would have to take it up with the officials. If my hon. friend had mentioned that he was going to bring up this case, I would have seen the officials in charge of it and tried to obtain the information he requires. He will understand that we have not all the details before us.
I have just given some details taken from the minister's own return.
The officials who dealt with this matter probably had reasons for taking the action they did. I should like to find out those reasons before I pass them on to the hon. member.

If the officials had any good reason for not making the appointment

it should appear in the evidence. I wish to make it clear that an inspector under the minister's supervision made a selection when he found the postmaster was short. After a delay of six months or so, the man he selected was officially appointed in response to public opinion in the community. Apparently the only difficulty was the fact that the defeated Liberal candidate in the constituency was not willing to recommend on the basis of efficiency, but recommended on some other basis which really did not satisfy even the local Liberal executive.
Where did you get that?

I read it in the return. The local Liberal executive was dissatisfied with the first appointment because he was a provincial government inspector. He had been an important factor in the last federal election, but he had left the community to go to another part of the province on provincial government business. He was unsatisfactory to the people in the community for that reason. The Post Office Department did not take any exception to the appointment of Mr. McGregor. As a matter of fact, they appointed him, and the inspector in Saskatoon, as is stated in the return, telephoned long distance to try to locate McGregor to find whether he was going to take the position.

As I understand it, the hon. member's complaint is that one of the officials of the department wrote to the defeated Liberal candidate to ask him for a recommendation, instead of accepting the man who was put temporarily in charge to carry on the office when the postmaster was removed because there had been a shortage of approximately $388. I understand that the hon. member is referring to the man who was actually appointed eventually. He was recommended in the first place by the post office officials.
Yes.
Was the revenue under $3,000?

The letter dated May 13 from E. J. Underwood, chief superintendent to J. Ross Barrie, Pelly, Saskatchewan, reads in part:
Would you be good enough to submit your recommendation, for the consideration of the Postmaster General, on the official form attached.
Male persons of military age are not eligible for appointment, but this restriction does not apply to returned soldiers.
What is wrong with that?

Nothing wrong about it except that the whole business was dragged out from April until the first week in January. Instead of acting on the advice of the inspector, the departmental administration wrote to the defeated candidate, who has never been in this chamber, who has never received the endorsation of the people of that community. I submit that the whole business is undemocratic and is not in the best interest of this country at this time. I think the Postmaster General should be prepared to give an undertaking that he will change that.

Am I to understand that, if in the distant future by some accident or some mischance my hon. friend's party should be on this side of the chamber, his party will not consult their defeated candidates about any appointments?

I wish to make it clear that if the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation cannot get a deputy postmaster general, an assistant deputy postmaster general and a staff of post office officials who can select capable and suitable postmasters and mail carriers, we will fire those who are available and we certainly will not have members of parliament making recommendations as to who will be postmasters, who will be mail clerks and who will be mail carriers. I am shocked to hear the Postmaster General make the admission that it is quite satisfactory to have a defeated candidate who has never been elected cause all this confusion in a community like Endeavour. It has affected the war savings campaign and the victory loan campaign. As I said before, the people judge the administration by what they see in their own back yard, and when this sort of thing goes on it does affect the contributions to other more worthy causes.

I listened to the declaration of the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, or the deputy leader, or the parliamentary assistant to the leader, as the case may foe,, but I always treat these declarations as being something that will never come to pass. The hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson) read a rather strange document which appeared in the sessional paper, a document containing an admission of liability to prosecution. Does this document represent the policy of the department? What is meant by an admission of liability to prosecution? Is there any special policy behind that? If a man is liable to prosecution, it seems to me that the department would become an accessory if it took such an admission and then went no farther. After

all, we have our criminal code. I think a serious responsibility rests upon the department to do something more than simply to leave that in the file. Perhaps something more was done in this case, but the sessional paper read by the hon. member does not indicate that.

Perhaps we can give more particulars when I have had an opportunity of taking this matter up with the officials. I understand that the form referred to has been in use in the department for many years; there is nothing new about it.
That makes it all the worse.
Apparently that has been the established system of the department for many years.

I do not care if it has been in use for fifty years. There is no reason to condone such a practice even though it is a long established usage. This is the kind of thing we ought to reform, and I think the minister would be well advised to give consideration to the position the department is in with respect to the matter.
That is being considered at the present time.
I am glad because it is a serious matter.

The statement I read appears at page 125' of Sessional paper 159. Will the minister state when his estimates are next before the committee., what has been done in this matter since Mr. B. Izdebski signed this statement on April 17, 1942?

I think I have made it clear that I shall inquire from the officials, and as soon as I hear from them I shall certainly make a statement.
